CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

TIME WINDOW: Today is 2026-10-06. Find developments published or posted
(journal articles incl. online-first, conference papers, arXiv / ChemRxiv /
SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from
2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06. You may include at most 3 especially important
items from 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, clearly labeled "earlier 2026". Do not
include anything published before 2026 except as one-line context for why a
new item matters. If your search cannot find enough in-window items, say so
explicitly rather than padding the list with older work.

QUESTION 3 - FEEDSTOCK, HIGH-THROUGHPUT FABRICATION, AND CHARACTERIZATION:
What new work is there on
(a) ultrasonic atomization of metal powders (e.g., AMAZEMET rePOWDER with
induction vs. plasma melting) - especially of refractory alloys, refractory
high-entropy alloys, Nb / Ta / W / Mo-based alloys, Ni superalloys, and
aluminum alloys - including powder yield, sphericity, oxygen pickup, and LPBF
performance compared with gas-atomized powder;
(b) small-batch or rapid alloy powder production for alloy discovery (e.g.,
plasma spheroidization, in-situ alloying from elemental or master-alloy powder
blends in LPBF / DED, compositionally graded builds), and how well
in-situ-alloyed specimens predict pre-alloyed behavior;
(c) high-throughput or miniaturized elevated-temperature mechanical testing
(miniature tensile, small punch, nanoindentation / micro-compression at
temperature, profilometry-based indentation plastometry, high-throughput creep
screening) and its correlation with bulk properties;
(d) automated / robotic characterization and ML-based analysis for AM alloys
(autonomous SEM/EDS/EBSD, automated metallography, in-situ melt-pool
monitoring as a low-cost fidelity level, X-ray CT defect quantification) that
could serve as cheap proxy nodes in a multi-fidelity loop.
For each, note whether it supports the "cheap proxy experiments vs. expensive
full tensile tests" cost hierarchy in the proposal, and give any quantitative
cost, time, or correlation numbers.

OUTPUT FORMAT: For each item give: full citation with DOI (or arXiv ID / URL),
the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain
exactly how, and how to reword the claim so it stays accurate);
[COMPETITOR] an active group or program likely to compete for the same money;
[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.

*Table: Key 2026 publications and preprints mapped to feedstock production, rapid alloy screening, miniaturized testing, and automated characterization. The final column identifies how each development supports—or qualifies—the proposed hierarchy of inexpensive proxy measurements and costly full-property tests.*

---

## (a) Ultrasonic Atomization and Refractory Alloy Powders

**1. Dodge, B.S., Niraula, S., Shokri, N., Gillham, J.D. & Berfield, T.A.** "Ultrasonic atomization of a refractory high-entropy alloy TiZrNbHfTa for additive manufacturing." *Powders* 5, 25 (Jul 2026). DOI: 10.3390/powders5030025. **Online: July 2026.**
This is the first reported ultrasonic atomization of a refractory HEA (TiZrNbHfTa) for AM, directly relevant to the PI's primary Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti system. It represents proof that small-batch ultrasonic atomization can process refractory compositions, a key enabler for the proposed pipeline.
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]** — Supports cheap feedstock node; the PI should cite this as validating the rePOWDER approach for refractory HEAs.

**2. Atabay, S.E., Baker, A.A., McKeown, J.T. & Voisin, T.** "Physical and microstructural properties of ultrasonically atomized nickel-tungsten (NiW) powders." *Mater. Des.* 269, 116623 (Sep 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.matdes.2026.116623. **Online: September 2026.**
Extends ultrasonic atomization to a high-melting-point Ni-W binary, evaluating powder morphology and microstructure. Relevant to the PI's secondary Ni superalloy system as it shows UA feasibility for refractory-element-containing Ni alloys.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Supports high-T feedstock feasibility.

**3. [earlier 2026] Bajaj, H.K. et al.** "Sustainable pathways in powder reuse: A comparative study of virgin, reused, and ultrasonic-atomization-recycled NiTi powder for additive manufacturing." *Sustainability* 18, 1843 (Feb 2026). DOI: 10.3390/su18041843. **Online: February 2026.**
This study explicitly uses the **AMAZEMET rePOWDER** UPA system at 40 kHz. UPA-recycled NiTi powder had D50 = 55.77 µm and mean sphericity = 0.93 (matching virgin powder), with a narrow span of 0.88 (bajaj2026sustainablepathwaysin pages 8-10). Cradle-to-gate energy was reduced from ~100 to ~50 MJ/kg (≈50%), with ~95% material recovery (bajaj2026sustainablepathwaysin pages 4-5). Oxygen was elevated relative to virgin powder under the system atmosphere used, highlighting the need for optimized inert-gas control. UPA energy was reported as 12–18 MJ/kg vs. 25–30 MJ/kg for conventional gas atomization (bajaj2026sustainablepathwaysin pages 4-5).
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER]** — Direct validation of rePOWDER platform and quantitative cost/quality metrics. Supports the cheap-feedstock node but flags oxygen control as a constraint requiring monitoring.

**4. Sojoodi, M. et al.** "Integration of circular economy into metal additive manufacturing: A review of ultrasonic plasma atomization for producing virgin and recycled NiTi powder." *Shape Mem. Superelasticity* 12, 5–45 (Oct 2026). DOI: 10.1007/s40830-025-00589-y. **Online: October 2026.**
Comprehensive review of UPA mechanisms. Reports sphericity indices often above 0.9, oxygen below 0.1 wt%, and 30–40% energy reduction vs. gas atomization (sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 2-3, sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 33-35). Higher ultrasonic frequency (40 vs. 20 kHz) refines particle size but slightly increases oxygen pickup (sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 33-35). UPA can process small 1–5 kg batches with 80–90% recovery (bajaj2026sustainablepathwaysin pages 4-5).
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Authoritative UPA background.

**5. Zhang, Y. et al.** "Process optimization of Nb521 powder via radio-frequency plasma spheroidization and its suitability for selective laser melting." *Int. J. Refract. Met. Hard Mater.* 138, 107742 (Aug 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.ijrmhm.2026.107742. **Online: August 2026.**
RF plasma spheroidization of a refractory Nb alloy (Nb521) with SLM suitability evaluation—a competing powder production route for refractory alloys.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Alternative refractory powder route to benchmark against UA.

**6. Feng, R. et al.** "Fabrication of lightweight TiNbCrAlVMoZr multi-principal-element alloy powder by RF plasma spheroidization." *Powder Technol.* 475, 122311 (May 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.powtec.2026.122311. **Online: May 2026.**
RF plasma spheroidization of a lightweight MPEA powder containing Nb, Mo, and other refractory elements.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Relevant feedstock for refractory alloy discovery.

---

## (b) Small-Batch Powder Production and In-Situ Alloying for Alloy Discovery

**7. Villapun, V.M. et al.** "Enabling alloy screening via multi-material printing using a production PBF-LB machine." *Prog. Addit. Manuf.* (Aug 2026). DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01939-7. **Online: August 2026.**
Demonstrates multi-composition screening on an unmodified production LPBF machine using a reduced-volume insert that limits powder usage to ~16% of the full build volume (villapun2026enablingalloyscreening pages 1-3). Five Ti-Cu compositions (0–20 wt% Cu in 5 wt% steps) were fabricated and evaluated in a single build. Hardness increased from ~199 to ~429 HV with increasing Cu content (villapun2026enablingalloyscreening pages 1-3). This directly supports the "cheap proxy experiments" paradigm: density cubes, hardness, and biological assays serve as inexpensive screening nodes before full tensile testing.
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER]** — Strongly supports the cost hierarchy; cite as validation that production PBF-LB can serve as a high-throughput alloy-screening node.

**8. Strauch, A.L., Altmann, M.L. & Toenjes, A.** "In situ alloying from powder blends enables processing of high copper content Ti-6Al-4V by laser powder bed fusion." *Discov. Mater.* 6 (Jun 2026). DOI: 10.1007/s43939-026-00738-9. **Online: June 2026.**
Blended Ti-6Al-4V + pure Cu at 10–20 wt% Cu; achieved up to 99.99% relative density and EDS-confirmed chemical homogeneity (strauch2026insitualloying pages 1-2). At 10 wt% Cu, robust processing was observed under all parameter sets; higher Cu increased cracking risk. This demonstrates that in-situ alloying can rapidly screen compositions, though it does not quantitatively compare against pre-alloyed behavior.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Supports feasibility of blend-based screening.

**9. Rodrigues, J. et al.** "Designing homogeneous Ti-Nb-Fe-Sn β titanium alloys by PBF-LB: A pre-alloyed powder blend strategy." *arXiv* 2609.17476 (Sep 2026). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.17476. **Online: September 2026.**
Proposes master-alloy powder blending (Ti-Nb, Ti-Nb-Fe, Ti-Nb-Sn) instead of pure elemental Nb to avoid incomplete dissolution and microsegregation typical of refractory element blends (rodrigues2026designinghomogeneoustinbfesn pages 1-5). Directly relevant to the PI's Mo-Nb-Ta-W system, where elemental blending of high-melting elements is problematic.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Informs feedstock strategy for refractory-element alloys.

**Additional items (unobtainable, noted from search metadata):**
- **Yeung, H. et al.** "Laser stirring with elliptical scanning enables on-demand alloying in additive manufacturing." *Addit. Manuf.* 118, 105101 (Feb 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2026.105101 — NIST work on in-situ alloying via scan-path control. **[CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR]**
- **Chmielewska, J. et al.** "A single-powder strategy for LPBF and LDED processing of a BCC Nb-Ti-Zr alloy." *J. Mater. Res. Technol.* (Nov 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jmrt.2026.09.099 — BCC refractory alloy from single pre-alloyed powder in both LPBF and LDED. **[CITE-FULL]**

---

## (c) High-Throughput and Miniaturized Mechanical Testing

**10. [earlier 2026] Moreno, D. et al.** "Anisotropy on mechanical properties of CMSX-6 Ni-base superalloy single crystal using profilometer indentation plastometer (PIP) and small punch test (SPT)." *J. Miner. Mater. Charact. Eng.* 14, 15–25 (Jan 2026). DOI: 10.4236/jmmce.2026.141002. **Online: January 2026.**
Applied PIP and SPT to a single-crystal Ni superalloy across three crystallographic orientations. PIP yield-strength estimates deviated ~10% from reference values; SPT empirical regressions achieved R² ≈ 0.89 for yield-related calibration, with combined PIP+SPT consistency within ~12% (moreno2026anisotropyonmechanical pages 8-10, moreno2026anisotropyonmechanical pages 5-8). This directly validates PIP/SPT as low-material proxy nodes for superalloys in the proposed cost hierarchy.
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER]** — Directly supports PIP/SPT as cheap proxy for Ni superalloy mechanical properties.

**11. Chawla, V., Penumadu, D. & Kalinin, S.** "Random combinatorial libraries and automated nanoindentation for high-throughput structural materials discovery." *Commun. Mater.* (Aug 2026). DOI: 10.1038/s43246-026-01294-8. **Online: August 2026.**
Introduces particle-based random combinatorial libraries containing hundreds to thousands of discrete compositions in one specimen, characterized by EDS mapping and automated nanoindentation guided by Gaussian-process/Bayesian optimization (chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 3-6, chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 1-3). Each indentation takes ~5 s; a 5×5 grid requires ~1280 s when avoiding the ~400 s reconfiguration penalty (chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 6-9, chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 20-23). The authors claim orders-of-magnitude throughput improvement over conventional synthesis-and-test workflows (chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 16-18). This is an extremely strong parallel to the PI's cost-aware multi-fidelity approach: nanoindentation as a cheap node, with cost-aware BO choosing measurement locations.
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER]** — Directly supports cheap proxy node concept with BO-guided testing.

**12. Wood, A.T. et al.** "Validation of profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP) testing for rapid qualification of electron beam–powder bed fusion (EB-PBF) with Ti-6Al-4V builds." *Adv. Eng. Mater.* (Apr 2026). DOI: 10.1002/adem.202502047. **Online: April 2026.**
AM-specific validation of PIP for rapid qualification of EB-PBF Ti-6Al-4V, establishing PIP as a quick surrogate for standard tensile tests on AM builds.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — AM-specific PIP validation.

**13. [earlier 2026] Zha, R. et al.** "HT-DABI: High-throughput extraction of creep and static material properties of metallic alloys via dimple array bulging." SSRN preprint 6169831 (Jan 2026). DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.6169831. **Online: January 2026.**
Introduces dimple-array bulging for high-throughput extraction of both creep and static mechanical properties—a missing intermediate fidelity level between room-temperature hardness and expensive long-duration elevated-temperature tensile/creep tests. Northwestern group (Cao, Espinosa, Dunand, McCue).
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER]** — Fills a critical gap in the cost hierarchy for elevated-temperature property screening. **[COMPETITOR]** — This Northwestern/Argonne group is actively developing HT methods for metallic alloys.

**14. Cannon, L., Davidson, K.P. & Quadir, M.Z.** "Evaluation of the small punch test: Repeatability and sample parameter influence." *J. Mater. Eng. Perform.* (Jul 2026). DOI: 10.1007/s11665-026-14603-6. **Online: July 2026.**
Establishes SPT repeatability for steels and derives empirical relationships to yield and ultimate tensile strength, supporting SPT use for rapid alloy screening including AM applications (cannon2026evaluationofthe pages 1-2).
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — SPT validation background.

**15. Muhit, M.M.I. et al.** "Hot isostatic pressing effects on multiscale mechanical properties and chromium-dependent strength retention in LPBF Fe-based shape memory alloys." *Sci. Rep.* 16 (May 2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-48695-w. **Online: May 2026.**
Uses PIP (ASTM 52965-25, 1 mm radius indenter) on LPBF Fe-SMA to compare as-built vs. HIP-treated conditions; cautions that PIP-derived tensile properties are effective/comparative rather than direct substitutes for conventional tensile tests under multiaxial conditions (muhit2026hotisostaticpressing pages 3-5).
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Important caveat for PIP in AM context.

---

## (d) Automated/Robotic Characterization and ML-Based Analysis

**16. Giri, S. et al.** "In-situ sensor monitoring of multi-class gas porosity formation in laser powder bed fusion using convolutional neural network." *J. Intell. Manuf.* (Apr 2026). DOI: 10.1007/s10845-026-02861-z. **Online: April 2026.**
Low-cost photodiode signals, calibrated against synchrotron X-ray ground truth, classify no-pore, small-pore (<15 µm), and large-pore (>15 µm) conditions with 79% accuracy, ROC-AUC = 0.89, and ~1 ms inference time per window (giri2026insitusensormonitoring pages 1-2). This is an ideal cheap proxy node: inexpensive sensors calibrated against costly diagnostics, enabling real-time quality assessment during builds.
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER]** — Directly validates in-situ melt-pool monitoring as a cheap fidelity level.

**17. Özel, T.** "Detection of anomalous meltpool conditions using deep learning in laser powder bed fusion." *Adv. Manuf.* (Jul 2026). DOI: 10.1007/s40436-026-00620-0. **Online: July 2026.**
ResNet-18/SVM hybrid classified normal, overheated, and underheated melt pools in Ni alloy 625 at 97.87% accuracy with ROC-AUC > 0.98 (ozel2026detectionofanomalous pages 1-2, ozel2026detectionofanomalous pages 15-16). Region-property extraction requires ~10 ms/frame. The system is designed for real-time feedback and parameter adjustment.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Supports melt-pool monitoring as inexpensive QC node.

**18. Cao, Z. et al.** "Physics-informed deep learning for virtual crystallographic phase and grain orientation reconstruction of additively manufactured alloys." Preprint, Aug 2026. DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10513494/v1. **Online: August 2026.**
PI-CycleGAN converts SEM secondary-electron images into virtual EBSD (band contrast, IPF, phase maps) across LPBF Ti-6Al-4V, 316L, Inconel 617, and Al 2219. Band-contrast reconstruction: mean SSIM > 0.64, PSNR > 22 dB, Pearson correlation > 0.82. Phase reconstruction: SSIM 0.83–0.92 (cao2026physicsinformeddeeplearning pages 11-13). This could reduce EBSD costs significantly by making standard SEM imaging a cheap microstructure-characterization proxy, with periodic real EBSD for calibration.
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER]** — Directly relevant: SEM as cheap node replacing expensive EBSD in the multi-fidelity loop.

2. **Chawla et al. (Aug 2026) demonstrated cost-aware, BO-guided automated nanoindentation on random combinatorial libraries.** This is a close conceptual parallel to the PI's multi-fidelity approach—nanoindentation as a cheap node, BO choosing where to measure next based on cost and information gain. Cite in the one-pager as support for the approach while differentiating the novelty of the BOFN formulation.

4. **Virtual EBSD from SEM (Cao et al., Aug 2026) and melt-pool CNN monitoring (Giri et al., Apr 2026; Özel, Jul 2026) provide quantitatively validated cheap proxy nodes.** Virtual EBSD achieves Pearson > 0.82 for band-contrast reconstruction (cao2026physicsinformeddeeplearning pages 11-13); melt-pool monitoring achieves 79–97.87% classification accuracy for porosity-related conditions (giri2026insitusensormonitoring pages 1-2, ozel2026detectionofanomalous pages 15-16). ## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current novelty claim reads: *"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty."*

**Recommended revision:** The 2026 literature shows that cost-aware BO and multi-fidelity proxy nodes are individually being adopted (Chawla et al. for combinatorial nanoindentation; Giri et al. for melt-pool-as-proxy; AlloyGen for LLM-automated CALPHAD; the NASA BO benchmark). However, no published work couples these concepts into a DAG-structured function network with partial evaluation across a complete powder-to-property AM pipeline. To maintain accuracy, consider rewording to:

*"While cost-aware Bayesian optimization and individual cheap-proxy measurements (e.g., automated nanoindentation, melt-pool monitoring) have recently been demonstrated for isolated alloy-screening tasks, no existing work integrates them into a unified directed acyclic graph of surrogate models spanning the full CALPHAD → atomization → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property pipeline. The core methodological novelty is the cost-aware, partial-evaluation optimization of this complete function network, where the algorithm dynamically selects which nodes to query—from cheap CALPHAD simulations and single-track experiments to expensive full tensile tests—based on expected information gain per unit cost."*

This revised wording (a) acknowledges the rapidly converging field, (b) sharpens the distinction between component-level demonstrations and system-level integration, and (c) is robust against the specific papers identified above.

**Additional note for reviewers:** The PI may also wish to add 1–2 sentences noting that recent work validates specific cheap nodes the platform will exploit: UPA powder sphericity ≈ 0.93 from the rePOWDER system (bajaj2026sustainablepathwaysin pages 8-10), PIP yield-stress estimates within ~10% of tensile values for Ni superalloys (moreno2026anisotropyonmechanical pages 8-10), and CNN-based melt-pool porosity classification at 79% accuracy with 1 ms inference (giri2026insitusensormonitoring pages 1-2). These quantitative correlations justify the multi-fidelity cost structure assumed in the BOFN formulation.

## Ranked Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

1. **Dodge et al. (Jul 2026) demonstrated ultrasonic atomization of a refractory HEA (TiZrNbHfTa) for AM.** This is the single most important paper for the proposal: it proves that UA/rePOWDER-type systems can process the exact class of refractory alloys proposed. The PI should obtain this paper immediately and cite it in the one-pager.

2. **Chawla et al. (Aug 2026) demonstrated cost-aware, BO-guided automated nanoindentation on random combinatorial libraries.** This is a close conceptual parallel to the PI's multi-fidelity approach—nanoindentation as a cheap node, BO choosing where to measure next based on cost and information gain. It validates the cheap-proxy paradigm but does not use function networks with partial evaluation of a manufacturing DAG. Cite in the one-pager as support for the approach while differentiating the novelty of the BOFN formulation.

3. **Zha et al. (Jan 2026, Northwestern/Argonne) introduced HT-DABI for high-throughput creep screening.** This fills the critical gap between room-temperature hardness and full elevated-temperature tensile/creep testing. The Northwestern group (Espinosa, Dunand, McCue, Cao) is a likely competitor for the same DOE BES or AFOSR funds. The PI should cite this as evidence that the community needs cheap intermediate-fidelity nodes and should consider whether HT-DABI could be incorporated as one such node.

4. **Virtual EBSD from SEM (Cao et al., Aug 2026) and melt-pool CNN monitoring (Giri et al., Apr 2026; Özel, Jul 2026) provide quantitatively validated cheap proxy nodes.** Virtual EBSD achieves Pearson > 0.82 for band-contrast reconstruction (cao2026physicsinformeddeeplearning pages 11-13); melt-pool monitoring achieves 79–97.87% classification accuracy for porosity-related conditions (giri2026insitusensormonitoring pages 1-2, ozel2026detectionofanomalous pages 15-16). These directly populate the low-cost nodes in the proposed DAG.

5. **AlloyGen (Taheri-Mousavi & Ni, Aug 2026) and the NASA BO benchmark (Stuckner et al., Mar 2026) signal growing competition in autonomous alloy design and BO-for-materials.** The PI's differentiator must be the coupled physical pipeline with cost-aware partial evaluation—not autonomous CALPHAD alone or generic BO for materials.

## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current novelty claim reads: *"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty."*

**Recommended revision:** The 2026 literature shows that cost-aware BO and multi-fidelity proxy nodes are individually being adopted (Chawla et al. for combinatorial nanoindentation; Giri et al. for melt-pool-as-proxy; AlloyGen for LLM-automated CALPHAD; the NASA BO benchmark). However, no published work couples these concepts into a DAG-structured function network with partial evaluation across a complete powder-to-property AM pipeline. To maintain accuracy, consider rewording to:

*"While cost-aware Bayesian optimization and individual cheap-proxy measurements (e.g., automated nanoindentation, melt-pool monitoring) have recently been demonstrated for isolated alloy-screening tasks, no existing work integrates them into a unified directed acyclic graph of surrogate models spanning the full CALPHAD → atomization → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property pipeline. The core methodological novelty is the cost-aware, partial-evaluation optimization of this complete function network, where the algorithm dynamically selects which nodes to query—from cheap CALPHAD simulations and single-track experiments to expensive full tensile tests—based on expected information gain per unit cost."*

This revised wording (a) acknowledges the rapidly converging field, (b) sharpens the distinction between component-level demonstrations and system-level integration, and (c) is robust against the specific papers identified above.

**Additional note for reviewers:** The PI may also wish to add 1–2 sentences noting that recent work validates specific cheap nodes the platform will exploit: UPA powder sphericity ≈ 0.93 from the rePOWDER system (bajaj2026sustainablepathwaysin pages 8-10), PIP yield-stress estimates within ~10% of tensile values for Ni superalloys (moreno2026anisotropyonmechanical pages 8-10), and CNN-based melt-pool porosity classification at 79% accuracy with 1 ms inference (giri2026insitusensormonitoring pages 1-2). These quantitative correlations justify the multi-fidelity cost structure assumed in the BOFN formulation.

CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from
2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06. You may include at most 3 especially important
items from 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, clearly labeled "earlier 2026". Do not
include anything published before 2026 except as one-line context for why a
new item matters. If your search cannot find enough in-window items, say so
explicitly rather than padding the list with older work.

QUESTION 3 - FEEDSTOCK, HIGH-THROUGHPUT FABRICATION, AND CHARACTERIZATION:
What new work is there on
(a) ultrasonic atomization of metal powders (e.g., AMAZEMET rePOWDER with
induction vs. plasma melting) - especially of refractory alloys, refractory
high-entropy alloys, Nb / Ta / W / Mo-based alloys, Ni superalloys, and
aluminum alloys - including powder yield, sphericity, oxygen pickup, and LPBF
performance compared with gas-atomized powder;
(b) small-batch or rapid alloy powder production for alloy discovery (e.g.,
plasma spheroidization, in-situ alloying from elemental or master-alloy powder
blends in LPBF / DED, compositionally graded builds), and how well
in-situ-alloyed specimens predict pre-alloyed behavior;
(c) high-throughput or miniaturized elevated-temperature mechanical testing
(miniature tensile, small punch, nanoindentation / micro-compression at
temperature, profilometry-based indentation plastometry, high-throughput creep
screening) and its correlation with bulk properties;
(d) automated / robotic characterization and ML-based analysis for AM alloys
(autonomous SEM/EDS/EBSD, automated metallography, in-situ melt-pool
monitoring as a low-cost fidelity level, X-ray CT defect quantification) that
could serve as cheap proxy nodes in a multi-fidelity loop.
For each, note whether it supports the "cheap proxy experiments vs. expensive
full tensile tests" cost hierarchy in the proposal, and give any quantitative
cost, time, or correlation numbers.

OUTPUT FORMAT: For each item give: full citation with DOI (or arXiv ID / URL),
the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain
exactly how, and how to reword the claim so it stays accurate);
[COMPETITOR] an active group or program likely to compete for the same money;
[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Integration of circular economy principles into additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a critical strategy for addressing economic and environmental challenges associated with the high-cost, resource-intensive production of NiTi shape memory alloys (SMAs). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) technique as an advanced recycling approach for converting NiTi AM waste into high-quality feedstock. Furthermore, UPA demonstrates significant potential as a dual-function method, enabling both alloying and fine powder production within a single integrated process. AM processes, such as powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB), binder jetting, and direct energy deposition (DED), often result in substantial material losses, exacerbated by powder degradation phenomena including oxidation, particle morphology changes, and loss of flowability. While conventional atomization techniques, such as gas and plasma atomization, offer partial solutions for powder production, they are limited by significant energy inefficiencies, high capital investment requirements, and increased risks of contamination. Moreover, powders produced via gas atomization typically exhibit inferior quality compared to those generated by UPA, including lower sphericity and a higher prevalence of surface satellites. In contrast, the UPA system, a hybrid technique combining high-frequency ultrasonic vibrations and plasma melting, offers precise control over droplet formation through acoustic cavitation, Faraday wave instabilities, and rapid solidification, enabling the production of highly spherical, homogeneous, and contamination-minimized NiTi powders. Drawing on thermofluidic principles, vibrational mechanics, and metallurgical kinetics, this review systematically deconstructs the UPA mechanism, highlighting key phenomena such as resonance-induced cavitation dynamics, ultrasonic capillary wave collapse, and non-equilibrium solidification. Furthermore, it investigates contamination pathways specific to UPA and proposes strategies for impurity mitigation, including sonotrode design optimization, inert atmosphere refinement, and post-atomization conditioning. Experimental findings are analyzed to demonstrate the feasibility of achieving high sphericity (> 0.9), compositionally stable, and thermally responsive NiTi powders from recycled feedstock. Finally, the review outlines a roadmap for industrial-scale deployment, advocating the integration of machine learning and closed-loop recycling models to enhance process predictability, quality control, and resource efficiency. The insights presented herein position UPA as a transformative solution for enabling sustainable, high-performance NiTi powder regeneration within AM workflows, advancing the circular economy in advanced manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Nickel–titanium (NiTi) shape memory alloys offer transformative functionality for biomedical and aerospace systems, yet their adoption in additive manufacturing (AM) remains constrained by powder reactivity, compositional sensitivity, and the high energy of feedstock production. This work establishes a unified, data-driven evaluation of how powder-state evolution during reuse and ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) affects both functional behavior and environmental performance. Virgin, reused, and UPA-recycled NiTi powders were systematically characterized based on particle-size distribution (PSD), SEM morphology, sphericity, oxygen content (ONH), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and these results were coupled with a process-level life-cycle assessment (LCA) spanning cradle-to-gate feedstock generation. Reused powder showed finer but broadened PSD, surface oxidation, and elevated transformation temperatures; these degradation mechanisms limited its reuse despite reducing energy demand by ~30% relative to virgin powder. UPA provided a more effective regeneration pathway: UPA-recycled NiTi recovered high sphericity and smooth particle surfaces while lowering cradle-to-gate energy from 100 ± 10 to 50 ± 5 MJ·kg−1 (≈50%) and reducing CO2-equivalent emissions by ≈45%, with ~95% material recovery. Although the UPA condition exhibited a higher oxygen content in this study due to system-level atmosphere limitations, prior work indicates that optimized inert-gas control can suppress oxidation, suggesting clear avenues for improvement. Sustainability Index analysis confirmed UPA as the most favorable route, integrating reductions in energy demand and emissions with recovery of powder morphology and reconditioning of thermal transformation behavior. More broadly, the ability of UPA to promote compositional and microstructural redistribution highlights its potential to deliberately re-tune or “reprogram” transformation temperatures for application-specific requirements when alloying and processing atmospheres are carefully managed.</jats:p>

In situ alloying from powder blends enables processing of high copper content Ti-6Al-4V by laser powder bed fusion Valid Text Names: 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 1-2', 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 2-4', 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 4-9', 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 9-11', 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 11-16', 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 16-18', 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 18-19', 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 19-20', 'strauch2026insitualloying pages 20-21' BibTex: @article{strauch2026insitualloying, author = "Strauch, Anna Luise and Altmann, Mika León and Toenjes, Anastasiya", title = "In situ alloying from powder blends enables processing of high copper content Ti-6Al-4V by laser powder bed fusion", year = "2026", journal = "Discover Materials", volume = "6", month = "Jun", doi = "10.1007/s43939-026-00738-9", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s43939-026-00738-9", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "1", issn = "2730-7727" } Abstract: Abstract Adding copper (Cu) to titanium (Ti) alloys or Ti-6Al-4V offers the potential to tailor microstructure and material properties, but previous studies report processing challenges for Cu contents above 5 wt%. In this work, Ti-6Al-4V powder was blended with pure Cu powder to investigate in situ alloying at 10, 15, and 20 wt% Cu using laser powder bed fusion. A systematic process parameter study was conducted, using identical parameters for all compositions, to evaluate the influence of Cu content on processability, density, and microstructural evolution. High relative densities (up to 99.99 %) and homogeneous, fine-grained microstructures were achieved, demonstrating that in situ alloying with Cu contents up to 20 wt% is feasible. While 10 wt% Cu could be processed robustly under all conditions, higher Cu contents showed an increased tendency for cracks. For 15 wt% and 20 wt% Cu, at least one set of parameters for each composition yielded a dense, crack-free sample. The microstructure was analyzed in detail using SEM to investigate the markedly different morphologies, while XRD was employed to identify the formed phases, including α- and β-Ti as well as Ti₂Cu. Mechanical properties were evaluated using Vickers hardness measurements (HV1) to compare the effect of Cu additions. EDS analysis confirmed chemical homogeneity across all blends. This work highlights the potential of powder blending combined with laser powder bed fusion to explore new Ti-6Al-4V–xCu compositions beyond previously reported limits. After contextualizing HEA/MHEA concepts and LPBF‑specific solidification phenomena, the review places particular emphasis on the modification strategies that tailor phase stability, melt‑pool behavior, and processability. These include targeted alloying additions, principal‑element ratio adjustments, and microalloying routes to stabilize FCC/BCC/B2 phase composition, mitigate cracking, and enable precipitation strengthening or microstructural refinement under LPBF’s rapid thermal cycles. A second major focus is the correlation between these compositional modifications and the resulting mechanical properties in both the as‑built and post‑processed conditions. The compiled data reveals distinct strength-ductility regimes across Cantor‑type alloys, Al‑containing dual‑phase systems, and refractory BCC‑based MHEAs, demonstrating how specific elemental additions, phase engineering strategies, and post‑processing treatments modulate hardness, tensile behavior, elongation, and failure modes. The comparative analysis highlights the strong dependency of mechanical properties on controlled phase fractions, segregation behavior, precipitates distribution, and defects. Overall, this review shows that the successful deployment of LPBF‑processed MHEAs critically depends on composition‑aware process design, where alloy modification strategies and mechanical property requirements must be jointly optimized. An Al-Si-Cu-Mg-Ni alloy for additive manufacturing from scrap mixtures: A combined high-throughput computational and 4D experimental proof of concept Valid Text Names: 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 1-7', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 7-11', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 11-14', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 14-21', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 21-26', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 26-31', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 31-35', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 35-40', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 40-45', 'bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy pages 45-47' BibTex: @misc{bugelnig2026analsicumgnialloy, author = "Bugelnig, Katrin and Strohmann, Tobias and Kolbe, Matthias and Becker, Michael and Navarrete, Nuria and Singh, Nisha and Lhuissier, Pierre and Villanova, Julie and Boller, E and Requena, Guillermo", title = "An Al-Si-Cu-Mg-Ni alloy for additive manufacturing from scrap mixtures: A combined high-throughput computational and 4D experimental proof of concept", year = "2026", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "Jun", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10115028/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10115028/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

A new Al alloy that can be processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) was discovered using a workflow combining computational high-throughput screening and experimental validation based on scrap metal mixtures. This workflow incorporates thermodynamic simulations, machine learning-assisted property prediction, optimization, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis, and experimental validation, accelerating alloy development while minimizing experimental effort. Complementary 3D/4D synchrotron-based characterization provided detailed insights into the microstructure, phase morphology, connectivity and porosity that go beyond the capabilities of simulations alone. Compared to conventional Al-Si alloys, the reduced Si-content of the identified alloy offers the potential to improve ductility, toughness and post-processing flexibility, all while maintaining reliable LPBF manufacturability.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) enables a level of design flexibility that is difficult to achieve with conventional techniques, yet it inherently yields materials marked by significant variability, anisotropy, and sensitivity to defects that challenge classical mechanics-of-materials assumptions. Process-driven microstructural heterogeneity, stochastic defect populations, and residual stresses strongly influence deformation, fatigue, and fracture behavior, often outweighing nominal material properties and constraining the predictive capability of traditional constitutive and fracture mechanics models. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful means of handling the complexity of AM data; however, many current approaches depend on black-box models that lack physical transparency, extrapolate poorly, and treat uncertainty inadequately. This review contends that ML should augment—rather than replace—mechanics-based modeling, and that dependable prediction of AM material behavior requires mechanics-informed ML frameworks. We critically analyze the central mechanics challenges in AM and evaluate established modeling strategies alongside emerging ML methods relevant to deformation, damage, fatigue, and fracture. Particular emphasis is given to physics-informed and hybrid ML approaches that explicitly incorporate anisotropy, defect sensitivity, residual stress effects, and uncertainty quantification within learning architectures. Recent progress in ML-assisted constitutive modeling, fatigue and fracture prediction, and digital twin development is synthesized, and the implications for qualification, certification, and structural deployment of AM components are discussed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The small punch test (SPT) is a fast method to evaluate alloys and compositional gradients across small length scales. However, its repeatability is commonly in question given size effects and sample preparation requirements. This study analyzes cold drawn commercial grade mild steels, correlating testing parameters to differences in microstructure and comparing them to the literature. The samples tested produced force–displacement curves that exhibited the expected five-stage deformation sequence. Low variance between tests proved sound sample preparation and testing techniques were used. Distinguished values of the curves were then used to develop an empirical relationship to known yield and ultimate tensile strength of the material and comparatively assessed with values from the literature. This relationship can now be applied to determine properties of SPT’s completed with similar steels. Results were analyzed further through a correlation matrix, showing a high relation between transition force and energy values of the test. Fractographic and microstructural analyses revealed ductile fracture mechanisms consistent with the steel’s properties. A heterogeneous spatial distribution of the strain field across a short length scale was observed, which emphasizes the critical requirement of metallographically homogenous structured samples for reliable data reproducibility.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Objectives.</jats:bold>
                    To summarize the results from studies of plasma processes for the production of specified composition powder materials; to implement plasma processes: plasma-chemical synthesis of nanopowders, granulation of nanopowders, plasma spheroidization of microgranules and micropowders in order to perform nanotechnologies and additive technologies tasks.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Methods.</jats:bold>
                    Thermal plasma generation was used at the A.A. Baikov IMET RAS by means of direct-current electric arc plasmatrons with a rated power up to 45 kW with self-adjusting arc length and gas stabilization of discharge, as well as plasmatrons with an interelectrode insert. In order to carry out the processes of nanopowders synthesis and metal powders spheroidization, the plasma reactor design with confined jet flow using thermal plasma of reducing, oxidizing, and inert media was used.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Results.</jats:bold>
                    The use of electric arc plasmatron in the processes of plasma chemical synthesis of nanopowders and plasma spheroidization of powders enabled productivity of 0.5 and 10 kg/h, respectively, to be achieved for various metals, alloys, compounds, and their compositions. In the case of the implemented processes of producing nanopowders, where the formation of particles depends on various macro-mechanisms, it was established that the average size of the particles obtained is controlled. This also depends on the synthesis parameters—the initial concentration of the precursor, enthalpy, and flow rate of the plasma jet, cooling rate and vapor condensation. The study shows the results of examining the processes of producing spheroidized powders in thermal plasma flows. These include (Ti, Ta, Fe, Ni, Mo, W), alloys (based on Fe, Ti, Ni, Co, Nb, W, Mg, including stainless, heat-resistant, refractory, hard), compounds (borides, oxides) and compositions (W–Ni–Fe, ZrB
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    –SiC, Ni–TiCN, etc.). The possibility of obtaining nonporous spherical powders of various dispersity was also shown: for particles of about 10–100 μm and for granules having a particle size of less than 1 μm. The study described the main process parameters determining the quality of spheroidization, including dispersity of precursor, plasma enthalpy, gas composition, characteristics of plasma flow, and their mixing with initial powders.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Conclusions.</jats:bold>
                    The research and development results presented here show the possibilities of plasma processes and apparatuses for producing nanopowders of various metal, inorganic compounds and compositions with given properties. The study also confirmed that powders of metals and alloys, compounds and compositions obtained by a variety of methods can be spheroidized in a plasma reactor with confined jet flow in a wide range of melting points, particle sizes, and morphology. The demonstrated approach using successive stages of plasma-chemical synthesis of nanopowders, their granulation and subsequent plasma spheroidization of microgranules enables tungsten-based composite micropowders with dense spherical particles and submicron structure to be obtained.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The mechanical characterization of welded joints is a critical step in assessing the structural reliability of stainless-steel components employed in marine, offshore, and industrial environments. Welding processes introduce significant local variations in microstructure and hardness, leading to heterogeneous mechanical properties that strongly influence fatigue life and structural performance. This study presents an integrated experimental–numerical methodology for the evaluation of local mechanical properties in AISI 316L butt-welded joints through minimally destructive hardness measurements. The approach combines two established hardness–property correlations to derive full true stress–strain curves for each region of the weld. These were subsequently implemented in a finite element model to reproduce the local and global deformation behavior during quasi-static tensile loading. Calibration was achieved using tensile tests on non-welded specimens, and a preliminary validation was conducted through Digital Image Correlation (DIC) strain measurements of both welded and base material specimens. Unlike most existing studies that focus on structural steels, this work investigates AISI 316L welds, austenitic stainless steel widely used in high-integrity applications, through a combined microhardness–FEM–DIC framework. The proposed methodology suggests the possibility to develop robust framework for correlating indentation hardness with mechanical response, offering a rapid, reliable, and potentially non-destructive route for assessing welded structures.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this work, the direct reuse of scrap from the addendum region of previously blow-formed aluminium sheets to manufacture smaller components through a secondary forming step was studied. Numerical simulations and experimental tests were conducted to assess the feasibility of the approach and to evaluate the behaviour of the pre-deformed blank and the thickness distribution of the secondary components. After primary forming, the selected scrap region exhibited less than 6% thinning and a maximum equivalent plastic strain of 0.11. The results showed that components produced from reused material exhibited thickness distributions comparable to those obtained from virgin sheet, with an average pointwise difference of approximately 3%. From an environmental perspective, the proposed closed-loop blow forming solution enabled substantial energy savings by avoiding the production of new sheet stock and the associated material-processing operations. The cradle-to-gate assessment showed that the scrap-based route reduced cumulative energy demand by 77% and global warming potential by 83% compared with the virgin-sheet route. These findings demonstrated that direct reuse of blow forming scrap via secondary forming can produce components with thickness distributions comparable to those obtained from virgin sheet while substantially reducing environmental impacts.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufacturing (AM) can fabricate, repair, and join near-net-shaped components for high-performance engineering applications, including biomedical, energy, and transport sectors. The broader adoption of DED remains constrained by the limited number of alloys available that can be reliably manufactured without imperfections, hence limiting mechanical properties. Here, we designed an Al–Ni–Ce–Mn–Fe AM alloy that can achieve an ultra-fine microstructure (<5 μm), uniform distribution of intermetallics, low residual stress (<32 MPa), and superior mechanical properties in as-built DED components. Compared to DED AlSi10Mg in the as-built state using the same conditions, the yield increased by 70%, and the ultimate tensile strength by 50%. DED-AM involves rapid cooling and complex thermal conditions, which largely influence the property of the final components. Post-characterization cannot capture the time resolved thermal behavior, hence offer limited mechanism-based guide for alloy design. In this study, we develop a novel multimodal characterization methodology for correlative in situ X-ray imaging, X-ray diffraction, and infrared imaging, enabling quantification of the in situ thermal-related behavior, including phase evolution, temperature distribution, and stress accumulation during DED. We elucidated key mechanisms driving the structure refinement and stress development in this alloy. The insights gained into the interplay between alloy composition, thermal-related behavior, and performance under specific AM conditions inform next-generation material design tailored for AM technologies.</jats:p>
