AI-Guided Self-Driving Laboratories for Advanced Materials Discovery Valid Text Names: 'mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 1-6', 'mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-12', 'mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 12-17', 'mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 17-22', 'mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 22-27', 'mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 27-31' BibTex: @article{mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories, author = "Mallia, Bernard and Caputo, Rossana", title = "AI-Guided Self-Driving Laboratories for Advanced Materials Discovery", year = "2026", journal = "Computing\&AI Connect", month = "Aug", doi = "10.69709/caic.2026.133382", url = "https://doi.org/10.69709/caic.2026.133382", publisher = "Scifiniti Publishing", issn = "3006-4163" } Abstract: Discovering new high-performance materials and alloys is often likened to finding a needle in a haystack because the design space of chemical compositions and processing conditions is astronomically large, and the discovery process is laborious and prohibitively costly. This perspective articulates a research agenda for autonomous materials and metallurgy discovery platforms that combine closed-loop machine learning with robotic experimentation and traditional materials engineering precepts to formulate, process, and test candidate materials with reduced human intervention, and to iterate recursively for stepwise optimization. It explores how sequential learning methods, generative modeling, and hybrid model-based strategies can analyze multimodal experimental data and propose new compositions and processing schedules for subsequent experiments. This approach has the potential to considerably accelerate the pace of discoveries, from decades to mere weeks. Representation learning for material formulations, the injection of domain knowledge into decision-making, and the mechatronic design of robotics that can safely execute harsh processing are all explored as essential components in closing the autonomous loop. Surveyed exemplars show order-of-magnitude improvements in experimental throughput and discovery efficiency. Furthermore, the paper proposes a multidimensional framework for classifying and evaluating the autonomy, complexity, and integration levels of self-driving laboratories, intended to give researchers and practitioners a structured approach to benchmarking future developments in the field. Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ceramics are valued for their high strength, thermal stability, and chemical inertness, but their structural applications are limited by intrinsic room-temperature (RT) brittleness. The stress required for dislocation motion in strongly ionic/covalent ceramics often exceeds their fracture strength, leading to catastrophic failure before plastic deformation occurs. Overcoming this limitation remains a major challenge in materials science. Recent studies have shown that ceramics exhibit RT plasticity through mechanisms including dislocation, phase transformation, and grain boundary sliding (GBS). These findings challenge the conventional view of ceramics as purely brittle materials and suggest that plasticity can be achieved not only in microscale specimens but also in bulk and structurally engineered ceramic systems. Several strategies have been developed to promote RT plasticity. Defect engineering, the controlled introduction and activation of dislocations, is critical for regulating deformation behavior. Structural designs such as coherent interfaces, layered architectures, and amorphous–crystalline composites can reduce dislocation nucleation barriers and improve deformation compatibility. Nanocrystalline structuring and external field regulation further enhance plasticity by altering local stress distributions and diffusion pathways. In situ characterization and strain measurement techniques have enabled direct observation and accurate quantification of deformation processes, improving the understanding of the relationship between structure, defects, and mechanical response. Despite these advances, achieving reliable and scalable plasticity in bulk ceramics remains challenging. Future work should focus on intrinsic plastic ceramic systems, scalable fabrication, and integrated multiscale design strategies. These efforts may enable the development of ceramics with improved damage tolerance and deformability for advanced structural and functional applications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

The excerpt compares profilometer indentation plastometry (PIP) and small punch testing (SPT) as miniaturized methods for characterizing anisotropic nickel-based single-crystal material and potentially additively manufactured metals. PIP uses a small ball, typically 0.5–1 mm in diameter, and probes a very localized region that may contain only one grain. SPT is more suitable for thin foils because the tested area samples more grains and can therefore provide more representative results. Both methods are affected by anisotropy, multiaxial stress and strain, grain sampling, and geometric constraints, and neither is an internationally standardized replacement for conventional tensile testing when sufficient material is available. The study tested <001>, <101>, and <111> orientations and found orientation-dependent yield stress and UTS trends consistent with established results. SPT estimates require forced empirical regression against external data; PIP-derived correlations showed fair agreement and approximately 10% deviation for yield stress. Calibrated alpha and beta coefficients may enable repeatable future measurements and production quality control for small AM specimens. The excerpt does not provide quantitative cost savings, testing-time reductions, or detailed comparisons with other miniaturized tests beyond PIP and SPT.

The excerpt describes photodiode-based thermal-emission monitoring as a low-cost, real-time proxy for defect detection in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Photodiode signals were collected simultaneously with high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging, allowing sensor signatures to be correlated with subsurface melt-pool dynamics and porosity ground truth. Continuous Wavelet Transform converted the time-series signals into time–frequency images, which were classified using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The system distinguished no pore, small pores below 15 μm, and large pores above 15 μm, with the threshold intended to separate relatively benign gas pores from structurally detrimental keyhole pores. Five-fold cross-validation produced 79% classification accuracy and an ROC-AUC of 0.89, with an average inference time of 1 ms per signal window. These results support the use of inexpensive in-situ sensors for scalable quality assurance, rather than relying exclusively on costly high-fidelity X-ray measurements. The excerpt does not explicitly describe a multi-fidelity optimization framework or quantify a specific porosity-correlation coefficient; however, the demonstrated relationship between affordable sensor data and X-ray-established porosity labels provides the basis for treating melt-pool monitoring as a cheaper, lower-fidelity level in such a framework.

CNNs address this nonlinear mapping by learning hierarchical defect precursors from thermographic or X-ray imagery and predicting porosity fraction, type distribution, and pore dimensions. From text 'chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 3-6'.

Vivek Chawla, Dayakar Penumadu, and Sergei Kalinin. Random combinatorial libraries and automated nanoindentation for high-throughput structural materials discovery. Communications Materials, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-026-01294-8, doi:10.1038/s43246-026-01294-8. This article has 1 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes random particle-based combinatorial libraries as substrates containing discrete microparticles, each with an independently assigned, uniform composition. Their stochastic arrangement enables hundreds to thousands of chemically distinct regions to be studied in a single specimen, unlike conventional gradient libraries whose compositions vary smoothly along limited spatial dimensions. EDS mapping and fiducial image registration provide chemical and spatial localization, allowing nanoindentation or other localized probes to associate mechanical measurements with individual compositions. The approach is intended to support high-dimensional materials discovery and automated Bayesian-optimization-guided measurement selection. Gaussian-process surrogate models estimate predictive means and uncertainties, while acquisition functions such as UCB and uncertainty estimation balance exploration, exploitation, and information gain. The stated throughput benefit is substantial: one indentation experiment could characterize mechanical properties across hundreds or thousands of compositions, with the proposed approach potentially increasing characterization rates by more than two orders of magnitude over sequential workflows. Cost savings are addressed conceptually through minimizing experimental cost and incorporating stage-motion costs into acquisition decisions, but the excerpt does not provide quantified dollar savings. It also does not report a specific correlation between measurements from the random libraries and bulk mechanical properties; instead, it emphasizes localized mechanical-property mapping and the practical limitations of particle size, probing volume, noise, spatial resolution, and reproducibility.

The workflow uses macro-to-micro EDS alignment, cluster-aware site selection, automated indentation, and Gaussian-process/Bayesian-optimization planning to balance exploration, uncertainty, and instrument-motion costs. A calibrated Monte Carlo framework accounts for minimum particle size, EDS noise and spatial resolution, positional accuracy, stage-motion penalties, and reconfiguration overhead. The article claims exponential reduction in the number of samples needed relative to conventional synthesis-and-test workflows and identifies regimes with orders-of-magnitude faster discovery. However, pages 1–3 do not provide numerical throughput rates, specific cost-savings figures, or quantitative correlation between nanoindentation measurements and bulk mechanical properties. The excerpt describes random combinatorial libraries as spatial mosaics of microscale particles or blocks, with each region assigned an independent composition from a high-dimensional design space. Simulated measurements are downsampled to effective EDS resolution and perturbed with Gaussian noise. The cost model includes nonlinear XY movement time and a manufacturer-imposed reconfiguration penalty of roughly 400 seconds when consecutive indents are more than approximately 1000 µm apart. A 5 × 5 grid takes about 1280 seconds when this penalty is avoided. Simulations impose motion limits to reflect instrument operation. The excerpt does not provide a measured correlation between nanoindentation results and bulk mechanical properties, explicit throughput rates beyond the 5 × 5-grid timing, or quantified cost savings; it only identifies related bulk-relevant properties as possible extensions and models time costs.

The excerpt describes a random combinatorial library made by embedding heterogeneous metallic machining particulates in conductive epoxy inside a brass ring. The uncontrolled alloy chemistries create a chemically diverse, high-dimensional library that can be characterized by EDS and tested by automated nanoindentation. EDS maps were acquired at high pixel density, downsampled eightfold to 200 × 256 pixels, and analyzed using elemental integration windows and nonnegative matrix factorization. The EDS map was registered to the nanoindenter through macro-to-micro alignment using two reference points, allowing map coordinates to guide stage navigation. K-means clustering of EDS compositions, with seven clusters selected by silhouette analysis, was used to reduce sampling bias toward abundant steel, copper, and brass particles. Candidate sites had to be at least 5 µm from particle boundaries and 50 µm apart; larger particles supported up to 100 sites. A Gaussian-process model guided the campaign after three randomly selected 3 × 3 grids, with ten exploratory grids using β = 2. Indents targeted 200 nm depth, and epoxy-associated measurements below 10 GPa were excluded. The excerpt does not provide quantitative correlation with bulk mechanical properties, indentation throughput rates, or cost savings; it only states that increasing library size increases total time without fundamentally preventing discovery.

The excerpt describes PI-CycleGAN, a physics-informed deep-learning framework for virtual EBSD characterization from a single grayscale SEM secondary-electron (SE) image. The model uses strain-induced SEM contrast together with crystallographic, boundary, and thermodynamic constraints to reconstruct physically consistent band-contrast (BC), inverse pole figure (IPF), phase, grain-boundary, and orientation maps. Its applicability was tested across additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4V, 316L stainless steel, Inconel 617 nickel-based superalloy, and 2219 aluminium alloy, spanning LPBF, LDED, and DED-Arc processes. Cross-system BC reconstruction achieved mean SSIM above 0.64, PSNR above 22 dB, and Pearson correlation above 0.82; grain-area, diameter, aspect-ratio, and circularity distributions also matched ground truth. Phase reconstruction produced SSIM values of 0.83–0.92, with an α-phase fraction correlation of 0.966 for 2219 aluminium. BC-to-IPF reconstruction achieved SSIM values of 0.65–0.81, PSNR of 23–30 dB, grain-level contrast correlation above 0.8, MAE below 0.09, and orientation colour errors generally near 15 or lower. The approach is intended for regions where conventional EBSD indexing fails or cannot resolve local microstructure.

The excerpt describes virtual EBSD reconstruction as a physics-informed, hierarchical image-translation problem that converts standard SEM secondary-electron images into EBSD-equivalent outputs: band-contrast maps, X/Y/Z inverse-pole-figure orientation maps, and phase-distribution maps. The motivation is that rapid solidification, steep thermal gradients, lattice distortion, dislocations, and residual stresses in additively manufactured alloys degrade Kikuchi-band quality and conventional EBSD indexing, creating local indexing blind spots. SEM images primarily capture etched morphology and chemical/topographic contrast rather than orientation directly, but grain size, grain positions, boundary topology, and etching responses are statistically coupled to crystallographic states. The proposed PI-CycleGAN imposes crystallographic and microstructural constraints to prevent visually plausible but physically invalid predictions, including violations of orientation relationships or crystal-symmetry-consistent IPF colors. Its progressive framework reconstructs microstructure, phase, and orientation in sequence through complementary subnetworks: MIN-CycleGAN for microstructure and BC maps, followed by phase-informed and crystallographic-informed components. Results are reported as consistent with real EBSD for additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4V, with comparisons against unconstrained and reduced-constraint models supporting the value of the physics constraints. The method is also reported to generalize to 316L stainless steel, aluminum alloys, and nickel-based superalloys.

The generated BC maps then serve as inputs to PhIN-CycleGAN for phase-map reconstruction and CIN-CycleGAN for crystallographic inverse-pole-figure (IPF) orientation maps, including IPFX, IPFY, and IPFZ. For Ti-6Al-4V, the framework is evaluated across the as-fabricated condition and annealed states at 950 °C/2 h and 1050 °C/2 h, using ground-truth EBSD maps for comparison. Reported evaluations include pixel residuals, grain-boundary consistency, SSIM, PSNR, FID, phase fractions, grain area, aspect ratio, circularity, equivalent diameter, grain contrast, and IPF colour error. Physics-informed extensions target three conversions: SEM SE to BC, BC to phase, and BC to IPF. Constraints enforce smooth yet sharp grain boundaries, intra-grain uniformity, realistic phase fractions and discrete phase assignment, valid IPF color space, physically reasonable grain-boundary misorientation, and reduced high-frequency noise. Three cross-domain tasks are identified: SEM SE-to-band-contrast (BC) reconstruction using MIN-CycleGAN, BC-to-phase reconstruction using PhIN-CycleGAN, and BC-to-IPF orientation reconstruction using CIN-CycleGAN. Their physical constraints include boundary smoothing, intra-grain consistency, edge preservation, frequency-domain consistency, dynamic phase distribution, phase discreteness, phase-boundary sharpness, IPF legal-colour-space restrictions, grain-boundary misorientation consistency, and total variation. Ablation results show that these constraints improve SSIM and PSNR and reduce distribution mismatch: FID decreases from 289 to 247 for SE-to-BC and from 88 to 63 for BC-to-phase. IPF reconstruction improves more modestly because crystallographic orientation fields are high-dimensional and non-unique. The physical basis is anisotropic etching: crystallographic planes dissolve at different rates, creating orientation-dependent microfacets and surface steps. SEM secondary-electron yield depends on local facet inclination and boundary edge effects, so grayscale contrast carries information about orientation, phase, and grain boundaries. Grain-boundary masking and watershed segmentation are used to reduce boundary noise and identify grains. The study presents a production laser-based powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) approach for screening alloys through in-situ formation of multiple compositions in one build, without modifying the machine. Specimens were evaluated rapidly with high-throughput mechanical and biological methods, including microhardness, non-destructive ultrasound, confocal imaging of pre-osteoblasts and mesenchymal stem cells, and assessment of Staphylococcus aureus. The approach is positioned against conventional research-scale alloy development, which typically uses vacuum arc melting, induction melting, or powder metallurgy to produce only 1–10 g ingots per day and follows a costly, time-consuming “one alloy at a time” process. {"answer": "# Question 3 — Feedstock, High-Throughput Fabrication, and Characterization: 2026 Developments

The following survey covers publications from 2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06, with up to three especially important items from earlier 2026 (January–March) explicitly labeled. The summary table below maps each item to the PI's sub-topics and cost hierarchy.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## (a) Ultrasonic Atomization and Refractory Alloy Powders

**1. Dodge, B.S., Niraula, S., Shokri, N., Gillham, J.D. & Berfield, T.A.** "Ultrasonic atomization of a refractory high-entropy alloy TiZrNbHfTa for additive manufacturing." *Powders* 5, 25 (Jul 2026). DOI: 10.3390/powders5030025. **Online: July 2026.**
This is the first reported ultrasonic atomization of a refractory HEA (TiZrNbHfTa) for AM, directly relevant to the PI's primary Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti system. It represents proof that small-batch ultrasonic atomization can process refractory compositions, a key enabler for the proposed pipeline.
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]** — Supports cheap feedstock node; the PI should cite this as validating the rePOWDER approach for refractory HEAs.

**2. Atabay, S.E., Baker, A.A., McKeown, J.T. & Voisin, T.** "Physical and microstructural properties of ultrasonically atomized nickel-tungsten (NiW) powders." *Mater. Des.* 269, 116623 (Sep 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.matdes.2026.116623. **Online: September 2026.**
Extends ultrasonic atomization to a high-melting-point Ni-W binary, evaluating powder morphology and microstructure. Relevant to the PI's secondary Ni superalloy system as it shows UA feasibility for refractory-element-containing Ni alloys.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Supports high-T feedstock feasibility.

**3. [earlier 2026] Bajaj, H.K. et al.** "Sustainable pathways in powder reuse: A comparative study of virgin, reused, and ultrasonic-atomization-recycled NiTi powder for additive manufacturing." *Sustainability* 18, 1843 (Feb 2026). DOI: 10.3390/su18041843. **Online: February 2026.**
This study explicitly uses the **AMAZEMET rePOWDER** UPA system at 40 kHz. UPA-recycled NiTi powder had D50 = 55.77 µm and mean sphericity = 0.93 (matching virgin powder), with a narrow span of 0.88 (pqac-00000000). Cradle-to-gate energy was reduced from ~100 to ~50 MJ/kg (≈50%), with ~95% material recovery (pqac-00000001). Oxygen was elevated relative to virgin powder under the system atmosphere used, highlighting the need for optimized inert-gas control. ## Ranked Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

1. **Dodge et al. (Jul 2026) demonstrated ultrasonic atomization of a refractory HEA (TiZrNbHfTa) for AM.** This is the single most important paper for the proposal: it proves that UA/rePOWDER-type systems can process the exact class of refractory alloys proposed. The PI should obtain this paper immediately and cite it in the one-pager.

2. **Chawla et al. (Aug 2026) demonstrated cost-aware, BO-guided automated nanoindentation on random combinatorial libraries.** This is a close conceptual parallel to the PI's multi-fidelity approach—nanoindentation as a cheap node, BO choosing where to measure next based on cost and information gain. It validates the cheap-proxy paradigm but does not use function networks with partial evaluation of a manufacturing DAG. Cite in the one-pager as support for the approach while differentiating the novelty of the BOFN formulation.

3. **Zha et al. (Jan 2026, Northwestern/Argonne) introduced HT-DABI for high-throughput creep screening.** This fills the critical gap between room-temperature hardness and full elevated-temperature tensile/creep testing. The Northwestern group (Espinosa, Dunand, McCue, Cao) is a likely competitor for the same DOE BES or AFOSR funds. The PI should cite this as evidence that the community needs cheap intermediate-fidelity nodes and should consider whether HT-DABI could be incorporated as one such node.

4. **Virtual EBSD from SEM (Cao et al., Aug 2026) and melt-pool CNN monitoring (Giri et al., Apr 2026; Özel, Jul 2026) provide quantitatively validated cheap proxy nodes.** Virtual EBSD achieves Pearson > 0.82 for band-contrast reconstruction (pqac-00000041); melt-pool monitoring achieves 79–97.87% classification accuracy for porosity-related conditions (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022). ---

## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current novelty claim reads: *"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty."*

**Recommended revision:** The 2026 literature shows that cost-aware BO and multi-fidelity proxy nodes are individually being adopted (Chawla et al. for combinatorial nanoindentation; Giri et al. for melt-pool-as-proxy; AlloyGen for LLM-automated CALPHAD; the NASA BO benchmark). However, no published work couples these concepts into a DAG-structured function network with partial evaluation across a complete powder-to-property AM pipeline. To maintain accuracy, consider rewording to:

*"While cost-aware Bayesian optimization and individual cheap-proxy measurements (e.g., automated nanoindentation, melt-pool monitoring) have recently been demonstrated for isolated alloy-screening tasks, no existing work integrates them into a unified directed acyclic graph of surrogate models spanning the full CALPHAD → atomization → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property pipeline. The core methodological novelty is the cost-aware, partial-evaluation optimization of this complete function network, where the algorithm dynamically selects which nodes to query—from cheap CALPHAD simulations and single-track experiments to expensive full tensile tests—based on expected information gain per unit cost."*

This revised wording (a) acknowledges the rapidly converging field, (b) sharpens the distinction between component-level demonstrations and system-level integration, and (c) is robust against the specific papers identified above.

**Additional note for reviewers:** The PI may also wish to add 1–2 sentences noting that recent work validates specific cheap nodes the platform will exploit: UPA powder sphericity ≈ 0.93 from the rePOWDER system (pqac-00000000), PIP yield-stress estimates within ~10% of tensile values for Ni superalloys (pqac-00000012), and CNN-based melt-pool porosity classification at 79% accuracy with 1 ms inference (pqac-00000018). These quantitative correlations justify the multi-fidelity cost structure assumed in the BOFN formulation.

BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->

surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

(journal articles incl. online-first, conference papers, arXiv / ChemRxiv /
SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from

items from 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, clearly labeled "earlier 2026". Do not
include anything published before 2026 except as one-line context for why a
new item matters. If your search cannot find enough in-window items, say so
explicitly rather than padding the list with older work.

What new work is there on
(a) ultrasonic atomization of metal powders (e.g., AMAZEMET rePOWDER with
induction vs. plasma melting) - especially of refractory alloys, refractory
high-entropy alloys, Nb / Ta / W / Mo-based alloys, Ni superalloys, and
aluminum alloys - including powder yield, sphericity, oxygen pickup, and LPBF
performance compared with gas-atomized powder;
(b) small-batch or rapid alloy powder production for alloy discovery (e.g.,
plasma spheroidization, in-situ alloying from elemental or master-alloy powder
blends in LPBF / DED, compositionally graded builds), and how well
in-situ-alloyed specimens predict pre-alloyed behavior;
(c) high-throughput or miniaturized elevated-temperature mechanical testing
(miniature tensile, small punch, nanoindentation / micro-compression at
temperature, profilometry-based indentation plastometry, high-throughput creep
screening) and its correlation with bulk properties;
(d) automated / robotic characterization and ML-based analysis for AM alloys
(autonomous SEM/EDS/EBSD, automated metallography, in-situ melt-pool
monitoring as a low-cost fidelity level, X-ray CT defect quantification) that
could serve as cheap proxy nodes in a multi-fidelity loop.
For each, note whether it supports the "cheap proxy experiments vs. expensive
full tensile tests" cost hierarchy in the proposal, and give any quantitative
cost, time, or correlation numbers.

the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain

[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.

## Ranked Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

1. **Dodge et al. (Jul 2026) demonstrated ultrasonic atomization of a refractory HEA (TiZrNbHfTa) for AM.** This is the single most important paper for the proposal: it proves that UA/rePOWDER-type systems can process the exact class of refractory alloys proposed. The PI should obtain this paper immediately and cite it in the one-pager.

2. **Chawla et al. (Aug 2026) demonstrated cost-aware, BO-guided automated nanoindentation on random combinatorial libraries.** This is a close conceptual parallel to the PI's multi-fidelity approach—nanoindentation as a cheap node, BO choosing where to measure next based on cost and information gain. It validates the cheap-proxy paradigm but does not use function networks with partial evaluation of a manufacturing DAG. Cite in the one-pager as support for the approach while differentiating the novelty of the BOFN formulation.

3. **Zha et al. (Jan 2026, Northwestern/Argonne) introduced HT-DABI for high-throughput creep screening.** This fills the critical gap between room-temperature hardness and full elevated-temperature tensile/creep testing. The Northwestern group (Espinosa, Dunand, McCue, Cao) is a likely competitor for the same DOE BES or AFOSR funds. The PI should cite this as evidence that the community needs cheap intermediate-fidelity nodes and should consider whether HT-DABI could be incorporated as one such node.

4. **Virtual EBSD from SEM (Cao et al., Aug 2026) and melt-pool CNN monitoring (Giri et al., Apr 2026; Özel, Jul 2026) provide quantitatively validated cheap proxy nodes.** Virtual EBSD achieves Pearson > 0.82 for band-contrast reconstruction (cao2026physicsinformeddeeplearning pages 11-13); melt-pool monitoring achieves 79–97.87% classification accuracy for porosity-related conditions (giri2026insitusensormonitoring pages 1-2, ozel2026detectionofanomalous pages 15-16). These directly populate the low-cost nodes in the proposed DAG.

5. **AlloyGen (Taheri-Mousavi & Ni, Aug 2026) and the NASA BO benchmark (Stuckner et al., Mar 2026) signal growing competition in autonomous alloy design and BO-for-materials.** The PI's differentiator must be the coupled physical pipeline with cost-aware partial evaluation—not autonomous CALPHAD alone or generic BO for materials.

## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current novelty claim reads: *"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty."*

**Recommended revision:** The 2026 literature shows that cost-aware BO and multi-fidelity proxy nodes are individually being adopted (Chawla et al. for combinatorial nanoindentation; Giri et al. for melt-pool-as-proxy; AlloyGen for LLM-automated CALPHAD; the NASA BO benchmark). However, no published work couples these concepts into a DAG-structured function network with partial evaluation across a complete powder-to-property AM pipeline. To maintain accuracy, consider rewording to:

*"While cost-aware Bayesian optimization and individual cheap-proxy measurements (e.g., automated nanoindentation, melt-pool monitoring) have recently been demonstrated for isolated alloy-screening tasks, no existing work integrates them into a unified directed acyclic graph of surrogate models spanning the full CALPHAD → atomization → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property pipeline. The core methodological novelty is the cost-aware, partial-evaluation optimization of this complete function network, where the algorithm dynamically selects which nodes to query—from cheap CALPHAD simulations and single-track experiments to expensive full tensile tests—based on expected information gain per unit cost."*

This revised wording (a) acknowledges the rapidly converging field, (b) sharpens the distinction between component-level demonstrations and system-level integration, and (c) is robust against the specific papers identified above.

**Additional note for reviewers:** The PI may also wish to add 1–2 sentences noting that recent work validates specific cheap nodes the platform will exploit: UPA powder sphericity ≈ 0.93 from the rePOWDER system (bajaj2026sustainablepathwaysin pages 8-10), PIP yield-stress estimates within ~10% of tensile values for Ni superalloys (moreno2026anisotropyonmechanical pages 8-10), and CNN-based melt-pool porosity classification at 79% accuracy with 1 ms inference (giri2026insitusensormonitoring pages 1-2). These quantitative correlations justify the multi-fidelity cost structure assumed in the BOFN formulation.

## (a) Ultrasonic Atomization and Refractory Alloy Powders

This is the first reported ultrasonic atomization of a refractory HEA (TiZrNbHfTa) for AM, directly relevant to the PI's primary Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti system. It represents proof that small-batch ultrasonic atomization can process refractory compositions, a key enabler for the proposed pipeline.
**Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]** — Supports cheap feedstock node; the PI should cite this as validating the rePOWDER approach for refractory HEAs.

Extends ultrasonic atomization to a high-melting-point Ni-W binary, evaluating powder morphology and microstructure. Relevant to the PI's secondary Ni superalloy system as it shows UA feasibility for refractory-element-containing Ni alloys.
**Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Supports high-T feedstock feasibility.

UPA-recycled NiTi powder had D50 = 55.77 µm and mean sphericity = 0.93 (matching virgin powder), with a narrow span of 0.88 (pqac-00000000). Cradle-to-gate energy was reduced from ~100 to ~50 MJ/kg (≈50%), with ~95% material recovery (pqac-00000001). ## Ranked Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

1. **Dodge et al. (Jul 2026) demonstrated ultrasonic atomization of a refractory HEA (TiZrNbHfTa) for AM.** This is the single most important paper for the proposal: it proves that UA/rePOWDER-type systems can process the exact class of refractory alloys proposed. The PI should obtain this paper immediately and cite it in the one-pager.

2. **Chawla et al. (Aug 2026) demonstrated cost-aware, BO-guided automated nanoindentation on random combinatorial libraries.** This is a close conceptual parallel to the PI's multi-fidelity approach—nanoindentation as a cheap node, BO choosing where to measure next based on cost and information gain. It validates the cheap-proxy paradigm but does not use function networks with partial evaluation of a manufacturing DAG. Cite in the one-pager as support for the approach while differentiating the novelty of the BOFN formulation.

3. **Zha et al. (Jan 2026, Northwestern/Argonne) introduced HT-DABI for high-throughput creep screening.** This fills the critical gap between room-temperature hardness and full elevated-temperature tensile/creep testing. The Northwestern group (Espinosa, Dunand, McCue, Cao) is a likely competitor for the same DOE BES or AFOSR funds. The PI should cite this as evidence that the community needs cheap intermediate-fidelity nodes and should consider whether HT-DABI could be incorporated as one such node.

4. **Virtual EBSD from SEM (Cao et al., Aug 2026) and melt-pool CNN monitoring (Giri et al., Apr 2026; Özel, Jul 2026) provide quantitatively validated cheap proxy nodes.** Virtual EBSD achieves Pearson > 0.82 for band-contrast reconstruction (pqac-00000041); melt-pool monitoring achieves 79–97.87% classification accuracy for porosity-related conditions (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022). These directly populate the low-cost nodes in the proposed DAG.

5. **AlloyGen (Taheri-Mousavi & Ni, Aug 2026) and the NASA BO benchmark (Stuckner et al., Mar 2026) signal growing competition in autonomous alloy design and BO-for-materials.** The PI's differentiator must be the coupled physical pipeline with cost-aware partial evaluation—not autonomous CALPHAD alone or generic BO for materials.

---

## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current novelty claim reads: *"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty."*

**Recommended revision:** The 2026 literature shows that cost-aware BO and multi-fidelity proxy nodes are individually being adopted (Chawla et al. for combinatorial nanoindentation; Giri et al. for melt-pool-as-proxy; AlloyGen for LLM-automated CALPHAD; the NASA BO benchmark). However, no published work couples these concepts into a DAG-structured function network with partial evaluation across a complete powder-to-property AM pipeline. To maintain accuracy, consider rewording to:

*"While cost-aware Bayesian optimization and individual cheap-proxy measurements (e.g., automated nanoindentation, melt-pool monitoring) have recently been demonstrated for isolated alloy-screening tasks, no existing work integrates them into a unified directed acyclic graph of surrogate models spanning the full CALPHAD → atomization → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property pipeline. The core methodological novelty is the cost-aware, partial-evaluation optimization of this complete function network, where the algorithm dynamically selects which nodes to query—from cheap CALPHAD simulations and single-track experiments to expensive full tensile tests—based on expected information gain per unit cost."*

This revised wording (a) acknowledges the rapidly converging field, (b) sharpens the distinction between component-level demonstrations and system-level integration, and (c) is robust against the specific papers identified above.

**Additional note for reviewers:** The PI may also wish to add 1–2 sentences noting that recent work validates specific cheap nodes the platform will exploit: UPA powder sphericity ≈ 0.93 from the rePOWDER system (pqac-00000000), PIP yield-stress estimates within ~10% of tensile values for Ni superalloys (pqac-00000012), and CNN-based melt-pool porosity classification at 79% accuracy with 1 ms inference (pqac-00000018). These quantitative correlations justify the multi-fidelity cost structure assumed in the BOFN formulation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes NiTi powder regeneration using an AmazeMet re-Powder® ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) system at the University of Toledo. The process combines localized plasma melting with high-frequency ultrasonic vibration to break up the melt and form spherical droplets. Used NiTi powder was fed into an argon plasma at a controlled rate; plasma power was selected to achieve complete melting while limiting evaporation and splashing. The system operated at 40 kHz, and rapidly solidified droplets were collected and sieved to 15–63 µm for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) compatibility. Compared with virgin and reused powder, UPA-recycled powder had a coarser but narrower particle-size distribution: D10 = 40.03 µm, D50 = 55.77 µm, D90 = 89.11 µm, and span = 0.88, versus virgin values of 16.68, 31.68, 50.58 µm and 1.07, respectively. Its mean sphericity was 0.93, matching virgin powder and slightly exceeding reused powder (0.92). The excerpt states that SEM was used to inspect surface quality, satelliting, oxidation, and particle integrity, while oxygen concentration was measured using ELATRA ONHp, but it provides no oxygen values. It also does not provide a direct comparison with conventional gas atomization or LPBF build-performance results. The process conditions were selected to balance powder quality, oxidation control, and energy efficiency.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited information specifically about ultrasonic atomization, ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA), AMAZEMET rePOWDER, refractory-alloy powders, or high-entropy-alloy powders. It characterizes UPA primarily as a recycling and circular-economy approach: it can convert unused AM powders, failed builds, support structures, and other scraps into reusable feedstock; operate under controlled inert-gas conditions that limit oxidation and harmful by-products; and reduce energy demand, emissions, and landfill burden relative to primary production from virgin materials. The excerpt does not report UPA-specific powder metrics such as sphericity, oxygen content, particle-size distribution, or LPBF results, nor does it identify AMAZEMET rePOWDER. For comparison, it gives conventional argon gas atomization (GA) data for NiTi: typical D50 is 20–100 µm, sphericity is 0.80–0.90, oxygen is approximately 0.02–0.05 wt%, nitrogen is generally below 0.005 wt%, and Hall flowability for well-sieved 15–63 µm powder is about 20 seconds per 50 g. GA-derived LPBF parts can reach approximately 99% density and 5–6% tensile recoverable strain, with transformation latent heat around 20–30 J/g. GA is scalable but can suffer Ni volatilization, crucible contamination, greater oxygen pickup in fine powders, and more satellite particles.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) for NiTi as a process combining ultrasonic vibration with thermal-plasma or induction heating. A molten stream contacts a sonotrode or vibrating plate operating at approximately 20–40 kHz; capillary-wave instabilities and acoustic cavitation fragment the melt into droplets, which solidify in an inert environment. Reported powder advantages over conventional gas atomization (GA) include finer mean particle size, narrower particle-size distribution, greater sphericity, lower porosity, and improved tap density and flowability. UPA is also associated with very low oxygen content, comparable to or better than conventional atomization, although higher ultrasonic frequency can increase surface-area exposure and cause a slight oxygen-pickup trade-off. Particle size can be adjusted through ultrasonic frequency and amplitude, with 40 kHz producing smaller particles than 20 kHz. Unlike GA, UPA can efficiently process small melts or molten scrap pools, making it relevant to recycling. The excerpt does not provide AMAZEMET rePOWDER-specific operating details, data for refractory or high-entropy alloy powders, quantitative sphericity or oxygen results, or direct LPBF performance testing. It only indicates that the resulting powder characteristics are favorable for powder-bed-fusion feedstock.

The ultrasonic energy induces standing capillary waves (Faraday instabilities) on the liquid surface, which, together with acoustic cavitation, lead to explosive disintegration of the liquid into fine droplets

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the operating principles of ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA), including its application to NiTi powder, but it does not provide specific AMAZEMET rePOWDER performance data, refractory- or high-entropy-alloy results, gas-atomization comparisons, or LPBF test outcomes. UPA combines a plasma torch, which creates a shallow molten film on a sonotrode, with high-frequency ultrasonic vibration. The vibration produces Faraday capillary waves, acoustic microstreaming, and cavitation; collapsing bubbles generate microjets and pressure pulses that destabilize the molten-metal surface and promote droplet ejection. Secondary breakup rounds the droplets, while rapid solidification in an inert plasma plume produces near-spherical powder. Particle size is linked to forcing wavelength and surface tension, and higher ultrasonic frequencies produce smaller droplets. Argon or another inert atmosphere limits oxidation, while rapid solidification supports compositional homogeneity. The excerpt identifies ultrasonic frequency and amplitude, plasma power, traverse speed, melt wetting, temperature, gas conditions, and solidification rate as key controls of throughput, particle-size distribution, sphericity, composition, and surface quality. It therefore supports qualitative claims about powder formation and quality, but contains no numerical sphericity, oxygen-content, or particle-size values and no direct evidence concerning LPBF performance or comparison with conventional gas atomization.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) for virgin and recycled NiTi powder, but it does not mention AMAZEMET rePOWDER, refractory alloys, high-entropy alloys, or provide dedicated LPBF test results. UPA combines high-frequency ultrasonic vibration with thermal plasma melting; acoustic cavitation and capillary-wave instabilities fragment molten NiTi, enabling controlled droplet formation and rapid solidification. Reported powders have high sphericity and homogeneity, with sphericity indices often above 0.9, narrow particle-size distributions, and few oxide satellites. Interstitial impurity levels are reported as oxygen below 0.1 wt% with minimal nitrogen, while recycled NiTi produced under high-purity argon reportedly retained acceptable oxygen levels and phase-transformation behavior comparable to virgin material. Increasing ultrasonic frequency from 20 to 40 kHz further refines particle size, although it can slightly increase oxygen pickup. Compared with conventional gas atomization, UPA can process much smaller melt pools or batches, offers in-situ composition adjustment, and reportedly reduces energy consumption by approximately 30–40%; however, its throughput is currently lower than high-volume gas atomization. The excerpt states that UPA-recycled powder achieved cleanliness, morphology, and functionality required for reuse in additive manufacturing, but it does not quantify LPBF density, tensile properties, defect rates, or other direct print-performance metrics.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides background on ultrasonic atomization (UA) and ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA), but it does not mention AMAZEMET rePOWDER by name or provide specific UPA experiments on NiTi, refractory alloys, or high-entropy alloys. It explains that ultrasonic waves oscillate the molten metal and reduce the relative importance of conventional nozzle and stream design. UA is associated with finer particle-size distributions and increased powder sphericity. For NiTi revert, the review distinguishes UPA from a true de-contamination process: like gas atomization (GA) and plasma atomization (PA), UPA does not remove internal oxygen or carbon already present in the melt, and powder chemistry remains strongly dependent on feedstock quality. The passage also notes that UPA remains sensitive to atmosphere and thermal exposure. Elsewhere in the excerpt, gas atomization is discussed as capable of producing chemically pure, predominantly spherical particles, while helium, gas recycling, and process optimization can improve efficiency. No quantitative oxygen-content, particle-size, sphericity, GA-comparison, or LPBF-performance results are included in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes in-situ alloying in LPBF as a flexible and potentially cost-efficient approach for screening new compositions by blending elemental powders and forming the target alloy during melting. Specifically, Ti-6Al-4V powder was blended with pure Cu powder at 10, 15, and 20 wt% Cu. Identical process parameters were used across compositions to systematically evaluate processability, density, and microstructural evolution. The approach produced relative densities up to 99.99%, homogeneous chemical distributions confirmed by EDS, and fine-grained microstructures. Ten wt% Cu was robustly processable, while 15 and 20 wt% Cu had greater crack susceptibility; nevertheless, at least one parameter set for each higher-Cu composition produced a dense, crack-free specimen. SEM, XRD, and Vickers hardness were used to assess morphology, phases (including α-Ti, β-Ti, and Ti₂Cu), and mechanical response. It states that PBF-LB can produce functionally graded materials and layered structures by varying composition, using either elemental or pre-alloyed powders mixed before deposition or fed separately through multiple hoppers. However, local homogeneity is considered essential even in intentionally graded builds, because particle-scale chemical variations can generate embrittling non-equilibrium phases or inclusions. For Ti-Nb systems, elemental blending is associated with incomplete dissolution of high-melting Nb, microsegregation, and local phase instability, potentially causing spatial variations in hardness, modulus, ductility, and damage tolerance. The study therefore proposes pre-alloyed master-alloy powders as an alternative: Ti-Nb, Ti-Nb-Fe, and Ti-Nb-Sn master alloys are blended with Ti to create multiple target compositions while avoiding pure refractory Nb particles and reducing local compositional extremes. contexts.context: The excerpt compares profilometer indentation plastometry (PIP) and small punch testing (SPT) as miniaturized methods for characterizing anisotropic nickel-based single-crystal material and potentially additively manufactured metals. PIP uses a small ball, typically 0.5–1 mm in diameter, and probes a very localized region that may contain only one grain. SPT is more suitable for thin foils because the tested area samples more grains and can therefore provide more representative results. Both methods are affected by anisotropy, multiaxial stress and strain, grain sampling, and geometric constraints, and neither is an internationally standardized replacement for conventional tensile testing when sufficient material is available. The study tested <001>, <101>, and <111> orientations and found orientation-dependent yield stress and UTS trends consistent with established results. SPT estimates require forced empirical regression against external data; PIP-derived correlations showed fair agreement and approximately 10% deviation for yield stress. Calibrated alpha and beta coefficients may enable repeatable future measurements and production quality control for small AM specimens. The excerpt does not provide quantitative cost savings, testing-time reductions, or detailed comparisons with other miniaturized tests beyond PIP and SPT.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides details only for profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP), not for small punch testing (SPT) or quantitative cost/time savings. PIP was used to estimate yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation by indenting the alloy with a hardened spherical indenter and using inverse finite-element modeling of the residual indentation profile to reconstruct an equivalent stress–strain response. The method followed ASTM 52965-25 and used a 1 mm-radius spherical indenter on specimens approximately 4 mm thick; residual profiles were measured with a stylus profilometer. Multiple indentations were conducted for repeatability, with reported properties averaged from individual inverse analyses. The authors caution that Fe-based shape memory alloys may deform through both plastic slip and stress-induced martensitic transformation, while indentation imposes a triaxial/compressive stress state rather than the uniaxial path of a conventional tensile test. Therefore, PIP values are effective or indentation-derived tensile properties intended mainly for comparative evaluation of as-built versus HIP-treated, remelted versus non-remelted, and chromium-free versus chromium-containing conditions, rather than direct substitutes for standardized bulk tensile measurements. Results were interpreted alongside Vickers hardness, nanoindentation, and densification data. No SPT methodology, correlation coefficients with bulk tensile properties, or cost/time-saving figures are included.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes PIP as a profilometry-based indentation method that uses the complete indentation profile, together with iterative finite-element inverse analysis, to infer mechanical properties. CORSICA software calculates true and engineering stress–strain curves and estimates yield stress, UTS, uniform elongation, and strain-hardening behavior using the Voce law. The principal limitation is the very small deformation volume: only a few grains may lie beneath the indenter, so crystallographic anisotropy can strongly affect results, particularly in single-crystal or anisotropic materials. The study performed at least three indentations and averaged the results. SPT uses a thin 0.7 mm specimen, a 4.763 mm chromium-steel ball, and load–displacement measurement in a stroke-controlled Instron machine. Yield and maximum loads are extracted from the punch-deflection curve. Empirical correlations relate SPT quantities such as Fe/t² and Fmax/(t·δ) to yield stress and UTS. In this work, correlations were constructed both from literature tensile data and from PIP-derived properties, allowing PIP data to calibrate SPT analysis while accounting for anisotropy. The excerpt does not provide quantitative cost or time savings, does not discuss additive-manufactured alloys specifically, and does not detail other miniaturized tests.

It identifies nano-indentation and profilometry-based plastometry (PIP) as rapid indentation methods that require less material and provide insight into material properties, but it does not describe PIP procedures, outputs, correlations, or quantified savings. The small punch test (SPT) is described in greater detail: it uses an approximately 8 mm diameter, 0.5 mm thick disk clamped in a die and punched using a miniature tool or 2.5 mm ball. PIP is presented as an alternative to conventional tensile testing when insufficient material is available, but it requires a minimum sample thickness of 3 mm and enough material for the indentation measurement. SPT is proposed for thinner components, such as blades, where PIP is impractical. SPT does not directly provide yield strength or ultimate tensile strength (UTS); instead, the study correlates SPT-derived quantities with tensile properties. contexts.context: The excerpt provides information on the small punch test (SPT), but not on profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP), additive-manufactured (AM) alloys, other miniaturized mechanical tests, or quantitative cost/time savings. In cold-drawn bright mild steels, an in-house SPT apparatus produced robust results with low test-to-test variation. Sample manufacturing was considered representative of the bulk material when the thickness-to-grain-size ratio was sufficiently high. Testing-parameter correlations showed a relationship between sample thickness and transition force (Fe), while microstructural differences—particularly Fe3C lath colony locations—produced larger effects and require consideration. Calculated SPT-based yield-strength and ultimate-tensile-strength estimates (bYS and bUTS) were compared with literature values, but the authors emphasized alloy-specific behavior and limited interchangeability, especially in carbon steels processed under different conditions. SEM observations indicated ductile fracture, involving localized deformation, void or pinhole formation, shear-band development, and radial cracking. Cross-sectional microscopy showed heterogeneous deformation across the disk, with distinct strain zones and an approximately 200-μm-wide yield-band region. Consequently, homogeneous sampling is essential for reproducible SPT data. No direct correlation coefficients with bulk tensile properties or numerical cost/time reductions are reported in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes two miniaturized mechanical characterization methods, but does not provide quantitative cost or testing-time savings for additively manufactured (AM) alloys. The Small Punch Test (SPT) uses a thin foil, typically about 0.5 mm thick, clamped between two dies while a hard ball applies increasing load until failure. Load and punch displacement are recorded, and empirical correlations use quantities such as yield load, maximum load, specimen thickness, and maximum deflection to estimate yield stress and ultimate tensile stress. The Profilometry-based Indentation Plastometer (PIP) measures the complete profile around a ball indentation and uses automated, iterative finite-element simulations to infer the material’s full true stress–strain curve, rather than relying on hardness alone. The paper applies both methods to CMSX-6 nickel-based single-crystal superalloy in the <001>, <101>, and <111> orientations to investigate anisotropy. It reports that combined PIP and SPT measurements produce consistent yield-stress estimates, with an estimated deviation below 12%. The introduction also mentions other small-specimen approaches, including ball punch/disk bend and shear punch tests, and notes that SPT was developed partly to characterize materials when only limited material—such as irradiated or previously tested specimens—is available. contexts.context: The excerpt describes photodiode-based thermal-emission monitoring as a low-cost, real-time proxy for defect detection in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Photodiode signals were collected simultaneously with high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging, allowing sensor signatures to be correlated with subsurface melt-pool dynamics and porosity ground truth. Continuous Wavelet Transform converted the time-series signals into time–frequency images, which were classified using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The system distinguished no pore, small pores below 15 μm, and large pores above 15 μm, with the threshold intended to separate relatively benign gas pores from structurally detrimental keyhole pores. Five-fold cross-validation produced 79% classification accuracy and an ROC-AUC of 0.89, with an average inference time of 1 ms per signal window. These results support the use of inexpensive in-situ sensors for scalable quality assurance, rather than relying exclusively on costly high-fidelity X-ray measurements. The excerpt does not explicitly describe a multi-fidelity optimization framework or quantify a specific porosity-correlation coefficient; however, the demonstrated relationship between affordable sensor data and X-ray-established porosity labels provides the basis for treating melt-pool monitoring as a cheaper, lower-fidelity level in such a framework.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes in-situ melt-pool monitoring in laser-based additive manufacturing using dual-wavelength thermographic imaging. Monitoring features included melt-pool length, temperature-distribution characteristics, and the number, size, and spatial distribution of spatters. These physically interpretable signatures were used with lightweight machine-learning models to classify porosity type—primarily lack-of-fusion and keyhole pores—and severity. A k-nearest-neighbor model achieved an F1-score above 95%, while a CNN trained directly on raw melt-pool images achieved F1-scores of 89–97%, indicating comparable predictive performance despite avoiding hand-crafted feature engineering. The excerpt emphasizes that simple, physics-informed monitoring can therefore approach the accuracy of more computationally intensive deep learning. However, conventional surface measurements do not provide a fully reliable direct correlation with porosity because pore formation depends on coupled hydrodynamic, thermocapillary, recoil-pressure, phase-transition, gas-entrapment, thermal-history, and instability effects that are not fully visible at the melt-pool surface. CNNs address this nonlinear mapping by learning hierarchical defect precursors from thermographic or X-ray imagery and predicting porosity fraction, type distribution, and pore dimensions. The excerpt does not explicitly discuss a multi-fidelity optimization framework or assign melt-pool monitoring a specific cheap fidelity level, but its lightweight models and lower computational burden support that potential use.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an in-situ, high-speed imaging system for monitoring meltpool conditions during nickel alloy 625 processing in an EOS M270 PBF-LB/M system. The proposed supervised method combines a ResNet-18 CNN with an SVM to classify normal, high-density-anomaly, and low-density-anomaly meltpools, reporting 97.87% accuracy. The framework is intended to reduce computational burden: region-property extraction requires approximately 10 ms per frame, nearly 100 times slower than the video frame rate, so detailed features are extracted only from frames first flagged as anomalous. Unsupervised k-means clustering using area, PBP, and SDPI produced groups corresponding to normal, high-density, and low-density conditions, supporting physically meaningful separation. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a random combinatorial library made by embedding heterogeneous metallic machining particulates in conductive epoxy inside a brass ring. The uncontrolled alloy chemistries create a chemically diverse, high-dimensional library that can be characterized by EDS and tested by automated nanoindentation. EDS maps were acquired at high pixel density, downsampled eightfold to 200 × 256 pixels, and analyzed using elemental integration windows and nonnegative matrix factorization. The EDS map was registered to the nanoindenter through macro-to-micro alignment using two reference points, allowing map coordinates to guide stage navigation. K-means clustering of EDS compositions, with seven clusters selected by silhouette analysis, was used to reduce sampling bias toward abundant steel, copper, and brass particles. Candidate sites had to be at least 5 µm from particle boundaries and 50 µm apart; larger particles supported up to 100 sites. A Gaussian-process model guided the campaign after three randomly selected 3 × 3 grids, with ten exploratory grids using β = 2. Indents targeted 200 nm depth, and epoxy-associated measurements below 10 GPa were excluded. The excerpt does not provide quantitative correlation with bulk mechanical properties, indentation throughput rates, or cost savings; it only states that increasing library size increases total time without fundamentally preventing discovery.

Monte Carlo simulations model an automated, cost-aware nanoindentation workflow. Random blocks are assigned compositions, a hardness field is generated, and noisy, pixelated EDS maps are reconstructed. A Gaussian-process surrogate uses interpolated compositions to guide Bayesian optimization, balancing predicted hardness, uncertainty, stage-movement time, and indentation time. Each selected region receives a 5×5 indentation grid, with simulated positional and measurement errors; the model is updated using the actual indentation locations. Runs end upon near-maximum hotspot discovery or after 100 global iterations. Many simulations discover the optimum within a few tens of iterations, while unsuccessful runs reach the 100-iteration limit, equivalent to approximately 35 hours of experimental time. Search difficulty is driven mainly by block number and block-size geometry; high block counts, very small particles, and larger positional errors hinder discovery. The excerpt does not provide quantitative correlation with bulk mechanical properties, measured throughput rates, or explicit cost-savings figures.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes PI-CycleGAN, a physics-informed deep-learning framework for virtual EBSD characterization from a single grayscale SEM secondary-electron (SE) image. The model uses strain-induced SEM contrast together with crystallographic, boundary, and thermodynamic constraints to reconstruct physically consistent band-contrast (BC), inverse pole figure (IPF), phase, grain-boundary, and orientation maps. Its applicability was tested across additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4V, 316L stainless steel, Inconel 617 nickel-based superalloy, and 2219 aluminium alloy, spanning LPBF, LDED, and DED-Arc processes. Cross-system BC reconstruction achieved mean SSIM above 0.64, PSNR above 22 dB, and Pearson correlation above 0.82; grain-area, diameter, aspect-ratio, and circularity distributions also matched ground truth. Phase reconstruction produced SSIM values of 0.83–0.92, with an α-phase fraction correlation of 0.966 for 2219 aluminium. BC-to-IPF reconstruction achieved SSIM values of 0.65–0.81, PSNR of 23–30 dB, grain-level contrast correlation above 0.8, MAE below 0.09, and orientation colour errors generally near 15 or lower. The approach is intended for regions where conventional EBSD indexing fails or cannot resolve local microstructure.
contexts.question: What are the details of virtual EBSD reconstruction from SEM images using physics-informed deep learning for additively manufactured alloys including Ti-6Al-4V, 316L stainless steel, aluminum alloys, and nickel-based superalloys?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes virtual EBSD reconstruction as a physics-informed, hierarchical image-translation problem that converts standard SEM secondary-electron images into EBSD-equivalent outputs: band-contrast maps, X/Y/Z inverse-pole-figure orientation maps, and phase-distribution maps. The motivation is that rapid solidification, steep thermal gradients, lattice distortion, dislocations, and residual stresses in additively manufactured alloys degrade Kikuchi-band quality and conventional EBSD indexing, creating local indexing blind spots. SEM images primarily capture etched morphology and chemical/topographic contrast rather than orientation directly, but grain size, grain positions, boundary topology, and etching responses are statistically coupled to crystallographic states. The proposed PI-CycleGAN imposes crystallographic and microstructural constraints to prevent visually plausible but physically invalid predictions, including violations of orientation relationships or crystal-symmetry-consistent IPF colors. Its progressive framework reconstructs microstructure, phase, and orientation in sequence through complementary subnetworks: MIN-CycleGAN for microstructure and BC maps, followed by phase-informed and crystallographic-informed components. Results are reported as consistent with real EBSD for additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4V, with comparisons against unconstrained and reduced-constraint models supporting the value of the physics constraints. The method is also reported to generalize to 316L stainless steel, aluminum alloys, and nickel-based superalloys.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the evaluation and training details of a physics-informed deep-learning framework for virtual reconstruction of EBSD-related modalities from microscopy data. The approach uses three constrained CycleGAN models: MIN-CycleGAN for backscattered-electron (BC) maps with microstructural constraints, CIN-CycleGAN for inverse pole figure (IPF) maps with crystallographic constraints, and PhIN-CycleGAN for phase maps with phase-field information constraints. BC-map reconstruction is assessed by comparing distributions of grain area, aspect ratio, circularity, and equivalent diameter between generated and real images. Phase-map reconstruction is evaluated through the predicted volume fractions of each phase. For IPF maps, grains are segmented using corresponding BC maps; average orientation vectors are calculated for each grain in generated and real maps, and grain-scale misorientation-angle distributions quantify preservation of crystallographic orientation. Each model was trained for 1,200 epochs. Batch sizes and learning rates were respectively 3 and 0.0002 for MIN-CycleGAN, 4 and 0.0001 for CIN-CycleGAN, and 1 and 0.0002 for PhIN-CycleGAN. Images were 256 × 256 pixels, and implementation used Python 3.12 with PyTorch 2.8 on an RTX 5070Ti workstation. This excerpt does not provide alloy-specific reconstruction results for Ti-6Al-4V, 316L, aluminum alloys, or nickel-based superalloys; Ti-6Al-4V appears only in a cited reference.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes physics-informed deep-learning reconstruction of EBSD-related maps from SEM secondary-electron images, with the clearest material-specific discussion focused on additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4V. Three cross-domain tasks are identified: SEM SE-to-band-contrast (BC) reconstruction using MIN-CycleGAN, BC-to-phase reconstruction using PhIN-CycleGAN, and BC-to-IPF orientation reconstruction using CIN-CycleGAN. Their physical constraints include boundary smoothing, intra-grain consistency, edge preservation, frequency-domain consistency, dynamic phase distribution, phase discreteness, phase-boundary sharpness, IPF legal-colour-space restrictions, grain-boundary misorientation consistency, and total variation. Ablation results show that these constraints improve SSIM and PSNR and reduce distribution mismatch: FID decreases from 289 to 247 for SE-to-BC and from 88 to 63 for BC-to-phase. IPF reconstruction improves more modestly because crystallographic orientation fields are high-dimensional and non-unique. The physical basis is anisotropic etching: crystallographic planes dissolve at different rates, creating orientation-dependent microfacets and surface steps. SEM secondary-electron yield depends on local facet inclination and boundary edge effects, so grayscale contrast carries information about orientation, phase, and grain boundaries. Grain-boundary masking and watershed segmentation are used to reduce boundary noise and identify grains. This excerpt does not provide reconstruction details for 316L stainless steel, aluminum alloys, or nickel-based superalloys.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a physics-informed, cross-domain deep-learning workflow for virtual EBSD reconstruction from SEM secondary-electron (SE) images. SEM SE images are first converted into EBSD backscattered-electron (BC) maps using MIN-CycleGAN. The generated BC maps then serve as inputs to PhIN-CycleGAN for phase-map reconstruction and CIN-CycleGAN for crystallographic inverse-pole-figure (IPF) orientation maps, including IPFX, IPFY, and IPFZ. For Ti-6Al-4V, the framework is evaluated across the as-fabricated condition and annealed states at 950 °C/2 h and 1050 °C/2 h, using ground-truth EBSD maps for comparison. Reported evaluations include pixel residuals, grain-boundary consistency, SSIM, PSNR, FID, phase fractions, grain area, aspect ratio, circularity, equivalent diameter, grain contrast, and IPF colour error. Comparisons are made against Pix2Pix, CycleGAN, and Paired-CycleGAN, while reduced-constraint experiments assess the contribution of the physics-informed restrictions. Figure 7 links SEM SE contrast to crystallographic orientation through anisotropic etching kinetics and topographical contrast. The method’s generalization is examined for additively manufactured 316L stainless steel, Inconel 617 nickel-based superalloy, and 2219 aluminium alloy, reconstructing BC, phase, and IPF maps and assessing image-quality, correlation, error, phase-proportion, grain-geometry, and orientation-colour metrics.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a virtual EBSD reconstruction workflow for additively manufactured alloys using paired SEM secondary-electron (SE) images and EBSD data. LDED-fabricated 316L stainless steel and Inconel 617 nickel-based superalloy samples, along with a DED-Arc 2219 aluminium specimen, were prepared by grinding, polishing, and alloy-specific etching; Ti-6Al-4V is mentioned as following similar standard metallographic procedures, but its detailed reconstruction results are not included here. SEM images and EBSD outputs—including band contrast (BC), phase, and IPF-X/Y/Z orientation maps—were spatially registered pixel by pixel. Original 1024 × 768 images were cropped into 256 × 256 patches, producing 384 paired datasets; augmentation and an 80/20 train-test split were used. The model is based on paired CycleGAN mappings and combines adversarial, cycle-consistency, identity, and paired-supervision losses. Physics-informed extensions target three conversions: SEM SE to BC, BC to phase, and BC to IPF. Constraints enforce smooth yet sharp grain boundaries, intra-grain uniformity, realistic phase fractions and discrete phase assignment, valid IPF color space, physically reasonable grain-boundary misorientation, and reduced high-frequency noise. Evaluation uses SSIM, PSNR, FID, grain morphology statistics, phase fractions, and orientation-related measures.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a deep-learning workflow for processing metallographic SEM/EBSD-derived image modalities, particularly band-contrast (BC), phase, and inverse-pole-figure (IPF) maps. BC maps are segmented into grains, after which grain area, aspect ratio, circularity, and equivalent diameter are extracted to compare morphology distributions between generated and experimental images. Phase-map performance is assessed by comparing the volume fraction of each phase. For IPF maps, grain regions are identified using corresponding BC maps; average grain orientation vectors are then calculated and compared through misorientation angles, producing a grain-scale orientation-error distribution that measures preservation of crystallographic information. Three constrained CycleGAN models support image generation: MIN-CycleGAN for microstructure-constrained BC maps, CIN-CycleGAN for crystallography-constrained IPF maps, and PhIN-CycleGAN for phase-field-constrained phase maps. Each model was trained for 1,200 epochs, with modality-specific batch sizes and learning rates, using 256 × 256 pixel images. The models were implemented in Python 3.12 with PyTorch 2.8 and executed on a workstation with an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D CPU, 64 GB RAM, and Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti GPU with 16 GB VRAM. The excerpt focuses on reconstruction and quantitative validation rather than full surface characterization of additively manufactured parts.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes deep-learning methods relevant to automated metallography and microstructure characterization from microscopy images. Few-shot learning can support rapid segmentation of electron-microscopy data when only a small number of labeled images are available, while 3D segmentation enables volumetric assessment of grain boundaries and phase distributions. Super-resolution models can convert low-resolution microscope images into higher-resolution representations, improving examination of nanoscale surface or phase distinctions. Vision foundation models such as Segment Anything (SAM), and its microscopy adaptation µSAM, are presented for segmentation and tracking in multidimensional microscopy data. A SAM-plus-few-shot workflow generated annotations from limited 2D images and achieved an 80.62% IoU on a 3D FIB-SEM tomographic dataset, although SAM may misinterpret abstract, noisy, or subtly contrasted material structures because it was trained primarily on natural images. The excerpt also notes experiments involving CLIP, DINOv2, and SAM on SEM and EBSD microstructure images. Explainable AI, including Grad-CAM, can identify phase boundaries and influential microstructural features, improving interpretability. Key limitations include scarce high-quality labels, overfitting from synthetic augmentation, restricted material and imaging diversity, and uncertain generalization. Additive-manufacturing-specific results are not provided in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited but related information about deep-learning-based image processing for materials characterization. It describes a multi-model framework that uses image-based descriptors together with thermal histories to model microstructural evolution in S235 steel from high-temperature confocal laser scanning microscopy data. A variational autoencoder (VAE) is used to compress microscopy images into a compact, low-dimensional representation. This compression improves computational efficiency and extracts features relevant to predicting phase transformation, but it also causes a controlled loss of spatial detail and reconstruction fidelity. The framework is conditioned on the specific initial surface, rather than reducing a heterogeneous material to generic descriptors, enabling predictions of both final Widmanstätten ferrite fraction and its temporal transformation behavior. The probabilistic model additionally quantifies uncertainty arising from experimental variability and noise. However, the excerpt does not provide specific methods, architectures, training procedures, evaluation metrics, or results for automated metallography, SEM images, EBSD images, segmentation of additively manufactured parts, or surface characterization. It mentions additive-manufacturing-related funding and future extensions, but the reported application is primarily high-temperature microscopy and phase-transformation forecasting.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes deep-learning methods applicable to automated metallography and characterization of manufactured-part microstructures, although it does not specifically identify additively manufactured parts. CNNs learn texture, edges, phase morphology, pores, and defect patterns from microscopy images. U-Net and DeepLab provide pixel-level segmentation by combining detailed spatial information with semantic features, supporting grain-boundary, phase, and pore segmentation. Faster R-CNN and YOLO localize and classify discrete features such as particles, pores, and phase regions; YOLO is particularly suited to rapid industrial inspection. Vision Transformers can model long-range spatial relationships and distributed defects. For SEM and related modalities, Pix2Pix can translate images between SEM and optical microscopy domains. GANs support realistic microstructure synthesis and data augmentation, while SRGAN and diffusion models can reconstruct or generate higher-quality microstructure images. EBSD analysis benefits from super-resolution, including enhancement of EBSD maps and reconstruction of higher-resolution orientation maps, potentially improving interpretation of material properties. U-Net-based extraction enables phase identification, while combined semantic segmentation and Watershed methods separate grain boundaries and phases. Explainable AI, including Grad-CAM, helps visualize model attention. Evaluation should consider precision, recall, F1-score, and precision–recall curves, especially when missed defects are more costly than false positives.
contexts.question: What are the details of AI-driven image processing for automated metallography, microstructure segmentation, and surface characterization of additively manufactured parts using deep learning on SEM and EBSD images?
